Immobilization due to fractures, burns, paralysis, or other causes is known to induce marked changes in calcium metabolism that may include hypercalcemia (>10.0 mg/dl), hypercalciuria (urinary calcium/creatinine ratio >0.3), elevated serum ionized calcium, and, if immobilization is prolonged, decreased total body calcium and loss of bone mineral density. It has been demonstrated that acute hypercalcemia during intravenous calcium infusion increases blood pressure and peripheral vascular resistance in both normotensive and hypertensive individuals. Whether or not alterations in calcium metabolism lead to immobilization-induced hypertension is less clear. If an immobilized patient develops hypertension, it is reasonable to assess serum total and ionized calcium, as ionized calcium may be elevated in immobilized patients even with normal total calcium levels.

Presentation: A 19-year-old female high school student presented with abnormal liver function for 2 years and was admitted to the hospital on October 17, 2018. Initially, she was found to have elevated alkaline phosphatase and γ-GT levels during a physical examination, despite being asymptomatic. Her liver function showed slight improvement after taking liver-protective medications (Ursodeoxycholic Acid and Bicyclol) as an outpatient. However, follow-up liver function tests remained abnormal. Due to her busy schedule and lack of symptoms, she initially refused hospitalization. Upon revisiting the hospital outpatient clinic on October 17, 2018, she was admitted after liver ultrasonography indicated cirrhosis. Upon admission, she exhibited no jaundice, pruritus, asthenia, anorexia, or other discomforts. She reported no history of alcohol intake or use of hepatotoxic drugs and had no family history of liver disease. Physical examination revealed mild splenomegaly, with other findings being unremarkable. Laboratory data from October 18, 2018, showed alanine aminotransferase at 62 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase at 45 U/L, alkaline phosphatase at 300 U/L, γ-GT at 119 U/L, total bilirubin at 14.9 μmol. Confirmed diagnosis: Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis type 3. Differential diagnosis includes: Progressive Familial Intrahepatic Cholestasis type 3.

Major stimuli for the synthesis of PTH in the parathyroid glands are hypocalcemia, low 1,25(OH)2D levels, and hyperphosphatemia, whereas hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia suppress PTH levels (Fig. 4). Finally, PTH levels are expected to be markedly elevated in children presenting with rickets due to CKD, which is usually associated with elevated serum phosphate and creatinine levels. Monitoring of PTH is an excellent marker for the response to therapy in patients with calcipenic rickets.

Studies have shown that sleep quality in young adults and middle-aged patients was heavily influenced by the surgical start time. Patients with surgeries that occurred in the afternoon (14:00–18:00) had increased levels of cortisol and decreased melatonin on postoperative night one than patients who underwent surgery in the morning, resulting in the afternoon group having almost twice the rate of sleep disturbances (70% of patients vs. 39%, respectively). Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is a condition where excessive amounts of bacteria typically found in the colon are found in the small intestine and result in various gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms. Patient with IBD, particularly Crohn’s disease, are at increased risk of SIBO. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the proportion of SIBO in patients with IBD was 22.3% (95% CI 19.92–24.68). The odds ratio (OR) for SIBO in patients with IBD was 9.51 (95% CI 3.39–26.68) compared to controls without IBD. The OR was significantly elevated in both CD (OR 10.86; 95% CI 2.76–42.69) and UC (OR 7.96; 95% CI 1.66–38.35). In subgroup analysis, patients with fibrostenosing CD (OR 7.47; 95% CI 2.51–22.20) and prior bowel surgery (OR 2.38; 95% CI 1.65–3.44), had increased odds of SIBO. Additionally, any structural factor that allows colonic bacteria to enter the small bowel, such as enterocolic fistulas or lack of an ileocecal valve can facilitate SIBO. The symptoms of SIBO are non-specific and non-predictive for SIBO, however commonly patients complain of bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, nausea, dyspepsia, diarrhea, and constipation. Diagnosing SUI based on classic symptoms can be easily confirmed during pelvic examination, by asking the patient to cough or Valsalva with a full bladder. If the provider observes urine leaking from the urethra during an office cough/Valsalva stress test, the diagnosis of SUI is confirmed. Urodynamic testing can also be performed to confirm a suspected diagnosis of SUI, however, based on the Value of Urodynamic Evaluation study, in women with uncomplicated SUI without significant prolapse or urinary urgency, if SUI is demonstrated on examination, additional urodynamic testing is not necessary before treatment. UUI is diagnosed by history and ensuring no acute cystitis, a normal post-void residual and normal screening urinalysis. Urodynamic testing may be considered if there are new-onset urinary symptoms and concern for pelvic nerve injury, such as in the setting of a prolonged second stage of labor or operative vaginal delivery. In women who have suspected bladder overdistension injury, urodynamics could help with diagnosis and determining prognosis, however, they are not mandatory.

Presentation: An 83-year-old man with a history of hypertension and asthma, and no prior abdominal surgeries, presented to the Department of General Surgery with an 8 × 8 cm necrotic area at the scrotal base. Nineteen years earlier, the patient had received radiation therapy twice over four years, totaling 82 Gy, for a condition in the same region. The patient was evaluated by colorectal surgeons, plastic surgeons, and urologists. The lesion was located at the scrotal base and featured a necrotic ulcer in the perianal area. Initial assessments considered the condition as a potential side effect of previous radiation therapy. Multiple biopsies were performed, and histopathological examination revealed specific findings without signs of invasiveness. Further clinical workup, including a normal colonoscopy and MRI of the lower abdomen, ruled out involvement of the urethra or corpora cavernosum.. Confirmed diagnosis: Primary perianal Paget’s disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Primary perianal Paget’s disease.

Presentation: A 42-year-old male with a history of cervical spine injury resulting in paraplegia since adolescence and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, as well as a small bowel obstruction treated with lysis of adhesions six months prior, presented with chronic abdominal pain and progressive abdominal distension over three months. His vital signs were stable and he was afebrile. Physical examination revealed a markedly tense abdomen with generalized tenderness and dullness on percussion. No signs of chronic liver disease were noted. Given his history of small bowel obstruction and the severity of his pain, a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. The CT scan showed no obstruction or perforation but revealed a large amount of loculated ascites, multiple adhesions with small bowel loops tethered to these adhesions, and hepatomegaly without evidence of cirrhosis or biliary tract obstruction. Laboratory results were as follows: calcium 8.7 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 650 IU/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, albumin 2 g/dL, globulin 5.3 g/dL, aspartate transaminase 20 IU/L, alanine transaminase 33 IU/L, and internationa. Confirmed diagnosis: Hepatic transthyretin amyloidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Hepatic transthyretin amyloidosis.

A physical exam may reveal an increase in abdominal girth and signs of bowel obstruction. Rectal and pelvic examination should be performed in constipated patients. Abdominal distention may be objectively assessed by abdominal inductance plethysmography, an ambulatory device that can continuously measure patients’ abdominal girth. Although there are no validated guidelines for the evaluation of FABD, the Rome IV 2016 working group recommends basic diagnostic tests such as complete blood count (CBC) if anemia is suspected, celiac serology (and if positive, duodenal biopsies should be added), abdominal x-ray to rule out obstruction, and a breath test for the diagnosis of SIBO.

Presentation: A 48-year-old male was admitted to Beijing YouAn Hospital with liver cirrhosis. Four months prior, an abdominal ultrasound indicated cirrhosis and splenomegaly, despite the patient experiencing no discomfort. At another hospital, he was diagnosed with diabetes and started on insulin therapy. The patient reported minimal alcohol consumption and no family history of liver diseases. Physical examination revealed skin pigmentation but no other abnormalities. Liver function tests showed elevated levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). Serum markers for viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver diseases were negative. Plasma iron indices were abnormal: iron at 47 μmol/L, transferrin saturation at 97.9%, and ferritin levels exceeding 2000 ng/ml. HbA1c was significantly elevated, while testosterone levels were normal at 18.26 nmol/L. Pre-contrast computed tomography (CT) showed hepatomegaly with increased attenuation in the liver and spleen, splenomegaly, and formation of collateral circulation. Differential diagnosis includes: Type 3 Hemochromatosis.

Presentation: A 55-year-old Caucasian male with a history of multiple myeloma currently undergoing chemotherapy with Velcade, Cytoxan, and dexamethasone, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, atrial flutter post-ablation, and melanoma of the left thigh post-surgical resection with negative lymph nodes and in remission, presented to the hospital with multiple episodes of nausea and vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, subjective fevers, and chills over the past 2 days. His last bowel movement was 2 days ago. On presentation, his vitals were stable. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel, were normal. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast showed a partial small bowel obstruction. A small bowel follow-through indicated non-specific thickening of the proximal small bowel loops. This was his third hospitalization with the same presentation of small bowel obstruction, with previous admissions one month ago and 2 weeks ago. During the initial hospitalization, an exploratory laparotomy showed no findings to suggest mechanical small bowel obstruction. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with push enteroscopy identified enteritis and a Mallory-Weis. Confirmed diagnosis: Gastrointestinal Amyloidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Gastrointestinal Amyloidosis.

Presentation: A three-day-old newborn male presented to the emergency department with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting starting on the second day after birth. Direct abdominal radiography and abdominal ultrasound did not reveal any abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests and thyroid hormone levels were within normal limits. A contrast enema radiography was conducted to investigate neonatal congenital bowel issues, but no abnormalities were detected. The patient resumed normal oral feeding for two days, after which vomiting recurred. Nasogastric intubation produced drainage containing fecalith, and there was an increase in abdominal distension, leading to the decision for an emergency operation.. Confirmed diagnosis: Ileum Duplication Cyst. Differential diagnosis includes: Ileum Duplication Cyst.

Which of the following is the most likely underlying etiology of this patient's symptoms?

Options:
A. Adhesions
B. Enteric nervous system damage
C. Impacted stool
D. Norovirus
E. Twisting of the bowel

Studies have shown that sleep quality in young adults and middle-aged patients was heavily influenced by the surgical start time. Patients with surgeries that occurred in the afternoon (14:00–18:00) had increased levels of cortisol and decreased melatonin on postoperative night one than patients who underwent surgery in the morning, resulting in the afternoon group having almost twice the rate of sleep disturbances (70% of patients vs. 39%, respectively). Diagnosing SUI based on classic symptoms can be easily confirmed during pelvic examination, by asking the patient to cough or Valsalva with a full bladder. If the provider observes urine leaking from the urethra during an office cough/Valsalva stress test, the diagnosis of SUI is confirmed. Urodynamic testing can also be performed to confirm a suspected diagnosis of SUI, however, based on the Value of Urodynamic Evaluation study, in women with uncomplicated SUI without significant prolapse or urinary urgency, if SUI is demonstrated on examination, additional urodynamic testing is not necessary before treatment. UUI is diagnosed by history and ensuring no acute cystitis, a normal post-void residual and normal screening urinalysis. Urodynamic testing may be considered if there are new-onset urinary symptoms and concern for pelvic nerve injury, such as in the setting of a prolonged second stage of labor or operative vaginal delivery. In women who have suspected bladder overdistension injury, urodynamics could help with diagnosis and determining prognosis, however, they are not mandatory.

Presentation: A 42-year-old male with a history of cervical spine injury resulting in paraplegia since adolescence and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, as well as a small bowel obstruction treated with lysis of adhesions six months prior, presented with chronic abdominal pain and progressive abdominal distension over three months. His vital signs were stable and he was afebrile. Physical examination revealed a markedly tense abdomen with generalized tenderness and dullness on percussion. No signs of chronic liver disease were noted. Confirmed diagnosis: Hepatic transthyretin amyloidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Hepatic transthyretin amyloidosis.

Presentation: A 48-year-old male was admitted to Beijing YouAn Hospital with liver cirrhosis. Four months prior, an abdominal ultrasound indicated cirrhosis and splenomegaly, despite the patient experiencing no discomfort. At another hospital, he was diagnosed with diabetes and started on insulin therapy. The patient reported minimal alcohol consumption and no family history of liver diseases. Physical examination revealed skin pigmentation but no other abnormalities. Liver function tests showed elevated levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). Serum markers for viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver diseases were negative. Plasma iron indices were abnormal: iron at 47 μmol/L, transferrin saturation at 97.9%, and ferritin levels exceeding 2000 ng/ml. HbA1c was significantly elevated, while testosterone levels were normal at 18.26 nmol/L. Pre-contrast computed tomography (CT) showed hepatomegaly with increased attenuation in the liver and spleen, splenomegaly, and formation of collateral circulation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a typical decrease in T2-weighted signal intensity over the liver.. Confirmed diagnosis: Type 3 Hemochromatosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Type 3 Hemochromatosis.

Presentation: A 55-year-old Caucasian male with a history of multiple myeloma currently undergoing chemotherapy with Velcade, Cytoxan, and dexamethasone, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, atrial flutter post-ablation, and melanoma of the left thigh post-surgical resection with negative lymph nodes and in remission, presented to the hospital with multiple episodes of nausea and vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, subjective fevers, and chills over the past 2 days. His last bowel movement was 2 days ago. On presentation, his vitals were stable. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel, were normal. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast showed a partial small bowel obstruction. A small bowel follow-through indicated non-specific thickening of the proximal small bowel loops. This was his third hospitalization with the same presentation of small bowel obstruction, with previous admissions one month ago and 2 weeks ago. During the initial hospitalization, an exploratory laparotomy showed no findings to suggest mechanical small bowel obstruction. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with push enteroscopy identified enteritis and a Mallory-Weis. Confirmed diagnosis: Gastrointestinal Amyloidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Gastrointestinal Amyloidosis.

Presentation: A three-day-old newborn male presented to the emergency department with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting starting on the second day after birth. Direct abdominal radiography and abdominal ultrasound did not reveal any abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests and thyroid hormone levels were within normal limits. A contrast enema radiography was conducted to investigate neonatal congenital bowel issues, but no abnormalities were detected. The patient resumed normal oral feeding for two days, after which vomiting recurred. Nasogastric intubation produced drainage containing fecalith, and there was an increase in abdominal distension, leading to the decision for an emergency operation.. Confirmed diagnosis: Ileum Duplication Cyst. Differential diagnosis includes: Ileum Duplication Cyst.

Studies were considered for eligibility if the population was gravida women with at least 1 prior CD, the diagnostic test was the absence of sliding sign in trans-abdominal ultrasonography, the reference test was surgical reports following CD and the outcome was existence of intra-abdominal adhesions involving the uterus. Intraabdominal adhesions in included studies involved any adhesions related to the access of the surgeons to the planned uterine incision (thin, filmy and easily separated adhesions by gentle, blunt or manual dissection with no vascular structures or adhesions between bowel or bladder and anterior uterine side making access to the lower uterine segment difficult and often require sharp dissection to release). Based on intraoperative findings, 4 levels of adhesions were identified: absent, mild (little or filmy adhesions), moderate (moderate to thick adhesions, require sharp dissection but do not involve bladder or bowel), and severe (absence of free space between uterine and abdominal walls or adhesions between uterus and bladder or bowel). A freely moving uterus indicated a low chance of adhesions (positive sliding sign). No uterine movement under the fascia of abdominal muscles suggested severe adhesions (negative sliding sign). US findings were compared to surgical reports following CD surgery as the reference standard test.

A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents for worsening symptoms of previously diagnosed acute sinusitis. Initially, the pediatrician prescribed decongestants and sent the patient home. Since then, the patient has developed a nasal discharge with worsening pain. The patient has a medical history of asthma which is well-controlled with albuterol. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 90/48 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Inspection of the patient's nose reveals a unilateral purulent discharge mixed with blood. The rest of the patient's exam is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Bleeding and infected vessel of Kiesselbach plexus
B. Foreign body obstruction
C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
D. Septal perforation
E. Sinusitis with bacterial superinfection

knowledge_chunks.text: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.

As respiratory pediatricians we all experienced that low-dose inhaled corticosteroids can easily control asthma symptoms in most of patients. Moreover, exacerbations in children are often concentrated in some periods of the year due to viral trigger or aeroallergens, and some little patients can even stop their treatment in summer time without clinical deterioration. Nevertheless, children and their parents sometimes keep complaining of recurrent respiratory symptoms despite the correct and continuous treatment, and various courses of antibiotics, beta-2 agonists and oral corticosteroids are frequently prescribed by pediatrician. As a consequence of the poor symptoms control, asthma treatment is often increased and the patient categorized as “problematic severe asthmatic.” However, an earlier step could be identified and this condition better defined as “problematic respiratory symptoms unresponsive to prescribed asthma therapy”. In fact, the known expression: “Not all that wheezes is asthma” continues to be relevant and the asthma diagnosis should be clinically reconsidered. In the last few decades, we possibly moved from under diagnosing to over diagnosing asthma. Presentation: A 29-year-old woman experienced recurrent bilateral purulent nasal discharge for 3 months. The symptoms began 3 months prior, accompanied by dizziness and headache. She had a cesarean birth at a local hospital 4 years ago and has no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed slightly congested mucosa in the bilateral nasal cavity, slightly enlarged inferior turbinates, hypertrophic middle turbinates, and a small amount of purulent nasal discharge in both middle nasal passages and posterior nostrils. Laboratory tests indicated slightly elevated serum uric acid (428.9 μmol/L), fibrin (4.9 g/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (30 mm/h), and ultrasensitive thyroid stimulating hormone (5.1 μIU/mL) levels, while myoglobin (< 21 ng/mL) was slightly decreased. Complete blood count, electrolyte profiles, and liver function were normal. A computed tomography scan from another hospital showed bilateral maxillary sinusitis, ethmoiditis, and bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy. A preoperative noncontrast chest computed tomography scan revealed a high-riding, tortuous structure extending to the mid-upper level of the first thoracic vertebra with local cystic dilatation, and a fe. Confirmed diagnosis: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery. Differential diagnosis includes: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery.

paranasal sinus fluid are done if sinusitis is the suspected source. Other laboratory tests are not

payload.vignette:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents for worsening symptoms of previously diagnosed acute sinusitis. Initially, the pediatrician prescribed decongestants and sent the patient home. Since then, the patient has developed a nasal discharge with worsening pain. The patient has a medical history of asthma which is well-controlled with albuterol. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 90/48 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Inspection of the patient's nose reveals a unilateral purulent discharge mixed with blood. The rest of the patient's exam is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Bleeding and infected vessel of Kiesselbach plexus
B. Foreign body obstruction
C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
D. Septal perforation
E. Sinusitis with bacterial superinfection

knowledge_chunks.text: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.

As respiratory pediatricians we all experienced that low-dose inhaled corticosteroids can easily control asthma symptoms in most of patients. Moreover, exacerbations in children are often concentrated in some periods of the year due to viral trigger or aeroallergens, and some little patients can even stop their treatment in summer time without clinical deterioration. Nevertheless, children and their parents sometimes keep complaining of recurrent respiratory symptoms despite the correct and continuous treatment, and various courses of antibiotics, beta-2 agonists and oral corticosteroids are frequently prescribed by pediatrician. As a consequence of the poor symptoms control, asthma treatment is often increased and the patient categorized as “problematic severe asthmatic.” However, an earlier step could be identified and this condition better defined as “problematic respiratory symptoms unresponsive to prescribed asthma therapy”. knowledge_chunks.text: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.

As respiratory pediatricians we all experienced that low-dose inhaled corticosteroids can easily control asthma symptoms in most of patients. Moreover, exacerbations in children are often concentrated in some periods of the year due to viral trigger or aeroallergens, and some little patients can even stop their treatment in summer time without clinical deterioration. Nevertheless, children and their parents sometimes keep complaining of recurrent respiratory symptoms despite the correct and continuous treatment, and various courses of antibiotics, beta-2 agonists and oral corticosteroids are frequently prescribed by pediatrician. As a consequence of the poor symptoms control, asthma treatment is often increased and the patient categorized as “problematic severe asthmatic.” However, an earlier step could be identified and this condition better defined as “problematic respiratory symptoms unresponsive to prescribed asthma therapy”. In fact, the known expression: “Not all that wheezes is asthma” continues to be relevant and the asthma diagnosis should be clinically reconsidered. In the last few decades, we possibly moved from under diagnosing to over diagnosing asthma. Nowadays, a thriving child with history of recurrent cough and a need of frequent beta-2 and inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) treatment is often diagnosed with “probable asthma” and ICS in ever increasing doses immediately prescribed. The initial suspected diagnosis, made with insufficient features and no spirometry testing, gradually, and with no evidence, becomes a definitive diagnosis rarely questioned in the fut

A hair visible in the skin ostium is considered to be pathognomonic for ND (Figure 1). NDs may be noticeable at birth, presenting as a lump or a pit on the nasal dorsum. The majority of them are diagnosed at infancy or in early childhood, but there are some reports of later diagnoses. A slow-growing mass may be observed in some cases in early infancy. Half of children may present hypertelorism and a broadened nasal bridge. Palpation may reveal a subcutaneous mass in 30% of patients, typically at the level of the osteocartilaginuous junction. Some authors have reported intracranial epidermoid and dermoid cysts in the proximity of the crista galli or foramen caecum without typical nasal manifestation. Recurring infections influence the long-term results of surgical treatment. Presentation: A 29-year-old woman experienced recurrent bilateral purulent nasal discharge for 3 months. The symptoms began 3 months prior, accompanied by dizziness and headache. She had a cesarean birth at a local hospital 4 years ago and has no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed slightly congested mucosa in the bilateral nasal cavity, slightly enlarged inferior turbinates, hypertrophic middle turbinates, and a small amount of purulent nasal discharge in both middle nasal passages and posterior nostrils. Laboratory tests indicated slightly elevated serum uric acid (428.9 μmol/L), fibrin (4.9 g/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (30 mm/h), and ultrasensitive thyroid stimulating hormone (5.1 μIU/mL) levels, while myoglobin (< 21 ng/mL) was slightly decreased. Complete blood count, electrolyte profiles, and liver function were normal. A computed tomography scan from another hospital showed bilateral maxillary sinusitis, ethmoiditis, and bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy. A preoperative noncontrast chest computed tomography scan revealed a high-riding, tortuous structure extending to the mid-upper level of the first thoracic vertebra with local cystic dilatation, and a fe. Confirmed diagnosis: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery. Differential diagnosis includes: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery.

Asthma diagnosis is often suspected when a constellation of typical features is present, however, as most guidelines highlight, diagnosis has to be confirmed either by objective tests or an objective response to treatment. One of the initial major error that occurs is that insufficient features of the asthma pattern are sought before the diagnosis is made. Patient's history should always give enough answers to the following question: “Does the child have any or all of cough, wheeze and breathlessness?.” A persistent cough (especially if non-productive) alone in an otherwise well-child is highly unlikely be due to asthma. The medical term wheezing is often used by parents to describe different sounds and care should be taken to be sure what they actually mean. Diagnosis is suspected clinically. Other disorders to consider include trauma, insect or animal bites

without cellulitis, retained foreign bodies, allergic reactions, tumors, and inflammatory orbital

pseudotumor.

Eyelid swelling may require the use of lid retractors for evaluation of the globe, and initial signs of

complicated infection may be subtle. An ophthalmologist should be consulted when orbital cellulitis is

suspected.

Preseptal cellulitis and orbital cellulitis are often distinguishable clinically. Preseptal cellulitis is likely if eye

findings are normal except for eyelid swelling. The presence of a local nidus of infection on the skin

makes preseptal cellulitis even more likely.

If findings are equivocal, if the examination is difficult (as in young children), or if nasal discharge is

present (suggesting sinusitis), CT or MRI should be done to confirm orbital cellulitis, to exclude tumor and

pseudotumor, and to diagnose sinusitis if present. MRI is better than CT if cavernous sinus thrombosis is

being considered.

The direction of proptosis may be a clue to the site of infection; eg, extension from the frontal sinus

pushes the globe down and out, and extension from the ethmoid sinus pushes the globe laterally and out.

Blood cultures are often done (ideally before beginning antibiotics) in patients with orbital cellulitis but are

positive in less than one third. Lumbar puncture is done if meningitis is suspected. Cultures of the

paranasal sinus fluid are done if sinusitis is the suspected source. Other laboratory tests are not

particularly helpful

payload.vignette:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents for worsening symptoms of previously diagnosed acute sinusitis. Initially, the pediatrician prescribed decongestants and sent the patient home. Since then, the patient has developed a nasal discharge with worsening pain. The patient has a medical history of asthma which is well-controlled with albuterol. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 90/48 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Inspection of the patient's nose reveals a unilateral purulent discharge mixed with blood. The rest of the patient's exam is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Bleeding and infected vessel of Kiesselbach plexus
B. Foreign body obstruction
C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
D. Septal perforation
E. Sinusitis with bacterial superinfection

payload.vignette:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with complaints of a sore throat and difficulty breathing. His mother reports that the symptoms began the previous night and have worsened rapidly. The child is normally healthy, up to date on all childhood vaccinations, and takes a daily multivitamin. His temperature is 103°F (39.4°C), blood pressure is 100/64 mmHg, pulse is 155/min, respirations are 29/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. On examination, he appears ill, is drooling, and leans forward to breathe. He is nonverbal, visibly uncomfortable, and does not cooperate with an oral examination. What is the most likely infectious cause of this patient’s symptoms?

Options:
A. Haemophilus influenzae
B. Streptococcus pneumoniae
C. Parainfluenza virus
D. Staphylococcus aureus
E. Group A Streptococcus
F. Adenovirus
G. Mycoplasma pneumoniae
H. Epstein-Barr virus
I. Corynebacterium diphtheriae
J. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)

Interpretation of findings:

Supraglottitis/epiglottitis and pharyngeal abscess pose a threat to the airway

and must be differentiated from simple tonsillopharyngitis, which is uncomfortable but not acutely

dangerous. Clinical findings help make this distinction.

With supraglottitis/epiglottitis, there is abrupt onset of severe throat pain and dysphagia, usually with no

preceding URI symptoms. Children often have drooling and signs of toxicity. Sometimes (more often in

children), there are respiratory manifestations, with tachypnea, dyspnea, stridor, and sitting in the tripod

position. If examined, the pharynx almost always appears unremarkable.

Pharyngeal abscess and tonsillopharyngitis both may cause pharyngeal erythema, exudate, or both.

However, some findings are more likely in one condition or another:

visible focal swelling in the posterior pharyngeal area (often with deviation of the uvula)

Although tonsillopharyngitis is easily recognized clinically, its cause is not. Manifestations of viral and

GABHS infection overlap significantly, although URI symptoms are more common with a viral cause. In

adults, clinical criteria that increase suspicion of GABHS as a cause include

Those with ≤ 1 criterion reasonably may be presumed to have viral illness. If ≥ 2 criteria are present, the

likelihood of GABHS is high enough to warrant testing but probably not high enough to warrant

antibiotics, but this decision needs to be patient-specific (ie, threshold for testing and treatment may be

lower in those at risk because of diabetes or immunocompromise). In children,

Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) may also present as ARDS. Hemorrhage can be bland (ie, not associated with vascular inflammation) or owing to capillaritis. In bland DAH, hemorrhage can result when elevated cardiac filling pressures (as in cardiogenic pulmonary edema) occur in the setting of coagulopathy or when contusion follows trauma. Alveolar hemorrhage owing to contusion should be considered when alveolar bleeding is coincident with pneumothorax, pneumatoceles, bony fractures, and cutaneous bruising. In contrast, capillaritis can be provoked by a wide range of insults including anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody–associated or other small vessel vasculitides, connective tissue diseases, anti–glomerular basement membrane disease, certain drugs, and infections.   Hemoptysis is a classic presenting symptom of DAH, although it is absent in at least one-third of patients, and a decrease in hemoglobin may also be observed. DAH is classically diagnosed by BAL showing an increase in red blood cells in serial lavage. Although DAD and DAH may have nearly identical radiologic appearances on the chest radiograph, highly experienced radiologists can sometimes make the diagnosis of DAH based on the differential radiodensity using a CT scan. The identification of DAH does not distinguish between bland hemorrhage and capillaritis, and should be followed by an investigation into the specific cause.

The distinction between acute and chronic stridor is important. Other clinical

findings are also often helpful (see

).

Acute manifestations are more likely to reflect an immediately life-threatening disorder. With these

disorders, fever indicates infection. Fever plus barking cough suggests croup or, very rarely, tracheitis.

Patients with croup typically have more prominent URI symptoms and less of a toxic appearance. Fever

not as stridor). Cough is often present with foreign body but rare with allergic reaction.

anomaly or an upper airway tumo

Two months prior, he had undergone surgery for diverticulitis of the large intestine at the same hospital and had recovered without complications. In the intensive care unit, fiberoptic laryngoscopy was performed to investigate the cause of his stridor and revealed immobile vocal cords in the paramedian position. A neurology consultation was requested to evaluate potential involvement of the lower cranial nerves. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spinal cord showed normal results, and cerebrospinal fluid studies ruled out infectious or inflammatory conditions. A tracheostomy was being considered to facilitate secretion management. The following day, during a re-examination, mild drooping of the left eyelid with positive fatigability was observed. pneumonia. Onset may be abrupt or gradual, with headache, anorexia, pleuritic or dull aching chest pain,

and generalized myalgia. Fever is usually > 39° C. Cough, tachypnea, and rales are characteristic.

Sputum may be blood-tinged. Chest x-rays usually show upper lobe consolidation, frequently cavitating

and resembling TB. Nodular lesions, thin-walled cysts, and pleural effusion may also occur. The WBC

count ranges from normal to 20,000/

μ

L.

begins abruptly, with septic shock and multiple organ involvement

manifested by disorientation, extreme dyspnea, severe headache, pharyngitis, upper abdominal colic,

diarrhea, and pustular skin lesions. High fever, hypotension, tachypnea, a bright erythematous flush, and

cyanosis are present. Muscle tenderness may be striking. Signs of arthritis or meningitis sometimes

occur. Pulmonary signs may be absent or may include rales, rhonchi, and pleural rubs.

not usually lead to shock.

Localized (chronic suppurative) infection

causes secondary abscesses, most often in the skin, lymph

nodes, or bone. Patients may be afebrile. An acute suppurative form is uncommon.

Supraglottitis/epiglottitis and pharyngeal abscess pose a threat to the airway

and must be differentiated from simple tonsillopharyngitis, which is uncomfortable but not acutely

dangerous. Clinical findings help make this distinction.

With supraglottitis/epiglottitis, there is abrupt onset of severe throat pain and dysphagia, usually with no

preceding URI symptoms. Children often have drooling and signs of toxicity. Sometimes (more often in

children), there are respiratory manifestations, with tachypnea, dyspnea, stridor, and sitting in the tripod

position. If examined, the pharynx almost always appears unremarkable.

Pharyngeal abscess and tonsillopharyngitis both may cause pharyngeal erythema, exudate, or both.

However, some findings are more likely in one condition or another:

visible focal swelling in the posterior pharyngeal area (often with deviation of the uvula)

GABHS infection overlap significantly, although URI symptoms are more common with a viral cause. In

adults, clinical criteria that increase suspicion of GABHS as a cause include

Those with ≤ 1 criterion reasonably may be presumed to have viral illness. If ≥ 2 criteria are present, the

likelihood of GABHS is high enough to warrant testing but probably not high enough to warrant

antibiotics, but this decision needs to be patient-specific (ie, threshold for testing and treatment may be

lower in those at risk because of diabetes or immunocompromise). In children,

Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) may also present as ARDS. Hemorrhage can be bland (ie, not associated with vascular inflammation) or owing to capillaritis. In bland DAH, hemorrhage can result when elevated cardiac filling pressures (as in cardiogenic pulmonary edema) occur in the setting of coagulopathy or when contusion follows trauma. Presentation: A 53-year-old male patient had a mitral valve replacement using a Starr Edwards metal valve. Post-surgery, he experienced acute renal failure and required temporary hemodialysis via a vascular catheter for 36 days. The longest duration a single catheter was used was 13 days. Cultures from four removed vascular catheter tips showed the presence of diphtheroids and coagulase-negative staphylococci, typically considered normal skin flora. During this period, the patient developed a low-grade fever, which subsided after changing the catheters. Blood cultures did not show any growth.. Confirmed diagnosis: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis caused by Corynebacterium jeikeium. Differential diagnosis includes: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis caused by Corynebacterium jeikeium.

Presentation: An 80-year-old female was admitted in March 2012 presenting with fever, low blood pressure, and confusion. Her medical history includes aortic valve replacement with a biological prosthesis and double coronary artery bypass performed in April 2011. Upon admission, blood cultures identified the presence of Staphylococcus lugdunensis. The patient was treated with oxacillin, which led to the resolution of her fever. CT/FDG-PET revealed a diffuse uptake on prosthetic valve (SUVmax 4.2). Two weeks after hospital admission a new TEE showed a peri-valve tissue abscess with aortic vegetation.. Confirmed diagnosis: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis.

The most common indication for TKR is osteoarthritis (OA). In 2018, 96.2% of primary knee replacements were conducted solely due to osteoarthritis. TKR helps to improve quality of life and function in end-stage, symptomatic osteoarthritis patients. However, 10–34% of TKR patients receive adverse pain outcomes between three months and five years following surgery and around 20% of TKR patients experience more knee pain and swelling than before surgery. Despite advancements in surgical techniques, prostheses, pain control, and medical care, there is evidence to suggest worsening pain and functional scores of some patients over time following TKR surgery.

 Polyarthritis + new murmur (endocarditis)
 Pediatric arthritis + fever + rash (consider Kawasaki disease , rheumatic fever , JIA)

Ventricular arrhythmias following Venus P-Valve implantation have been reported predominantly as transient, early events. In a recent multicenter comparative study by Haddad et al. (2025; n = 145), directly comparing self-expanding Venus P-Valve (n = 52) with balloon-expandable SAPIEN-3 (n = 93) in native or patched RVOTs, procedural success was 100% in both groups and major complication rates were comparable (9.6%, 5/52, in the Venus-P cohort). Transient ventricular arrhythmias occurred more frequently after Venus P-Valve implantation (21.1%, 11/52) compared with SAPIEN-3 (3.2%, 3/93), but all events resolved without catheter ablation or long-term antiarrhythmic therapy, and no sustained ventricular tachycardia or arrhythmic death was reported. Across additional multicenter and registry experiences, sustained ventricular arrhythmias have been uncommon. In the Italian SICPED Registry, transient ventricular ectopy – occasionally short non-sustained ventricular tachycardia – was observed in 19% (12/65) of patients, typically resolving within one month on β-blocker therapy, with no cases of high-grade atrioventricular block, pacemaker implantation, or sudden arrhythmic death at a median 13-month follow-up. Splenomegaly is the hallmark; spleen size correlates with the degree of anemia. The spleen can be

expected to extend about 2 cm beneath the costal margin for each 1-g decrease in Hb. Other clinical

findings usually result from the underlying disorder.

Although type 1 diabetes also exhibits increased hepatic gluconeogenesis, hyperglucagonemia and hyperglycemia, it is not a risk factor for NAFLD. This can be attributed to the absence of glucagon resistance in type 1 diabetes, as manifested by increased hepatic urea synthesis efficiency. In type 1 diabetes, hyperglucagonemia and associated hyperglycemia occur because of reduced insulin secretion. Notably, hyperinsulinemia, a characteristic of type 2 but not type 1 diabetes, causes reduced plasma adiponectin. On the other hand, patients with type 1 diabetes have increased plasma adiponectin. Adiponectin signaling in hepatocytes activates AMPK and improves insulin sensitivity. AMPK activation should inhibit all the components of glucagon resistance including lipogenesis (Figure 4). AMPK activates endothelial nitric oxide synthase, which produces nitric oxide, which inhibits xanthine oxidase. Hence, type 1 diabetes is also associated with reduced uric acid synthesis.

US is the most validated modality for assessing splenomegaly. The splenic volume is calculated using the formula for a prolate ellipse (0.52 × length × anteroposterior dimension × width). However, given the strong correlation between the splenic length and volume, a simple measurement of the longest dimension along the oblique craniocaudal axis is preferred. In contrast, CT and MRI, which provide images on predefined planes, may underestimate splenic size because of challenges in accurately measuring the longest craniocaudal dimension. Chow et al. conducted a study aimed at defining individualized normal values for splenic length and volume. They found that splenic size correlates with height, weight, and sex: it tends to be larger in taller, heavier individuals and in males. Notably, the frequently cited upper limit of normal for splenic length (12 cm) was exceeded by 26% of males and 6% of females. This finding highlights the need for corrected upper limits to prevent unnecessary workups in otherwise healthy individuals whose splenic length surpasses the published normal values. They also proposed validated algorithms to determine the percentiles of individual splenic sizes and introduced an application to facilitate clinical use (for iOS [https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/splenocalc/id1005559584?mt=8] and Android [https://play.google.com/store/search?q=splenocalc]).

Hyperinsulinism is a medical condition characterized by inappropriately high insulin secretion compared to plasma glucose concentration, leading to a continuous stimulation of hepatic glycogen synthesis and glucose uptake by skeletal muscles and adipose tissue. Hyperinsulinism can be transient, congenital or syndromic. Transient hyperinsulinism is a common cause of severe hypoglycemia in newborns and it can be found in children of diabetic mothers, IUGR, SGA or it can be secondary to perinatal stress. The disease course is usually self-limiting and it is defined by resolution prior to 6 months of age. Hyperinsulinism in infants of diabetic mothers, when diabetes in poorly controlled, is caused by prolonged intrauterine exposure to high blood glucose levels resulting in increased fetal growth and LGA. Immediately after birth, these infants are at high risk for hypoglycemia but, usually, this condition resolves spontaneously in a few days until the beta-pancreatic cells adapt to the normoglycemic state. In addition, gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is associated with long-term complications for offspring including childhood obesity and glucose intolerance. The molecular basis of offspring adiposity and glucose intolerance is expected to be correlated to genetic and epigenetic modifications owing to intrauterine hyperglycemia. In some cases, newborns experience a prolonged state of transient hyperinsulinism. This disorder seems to occur primarily in SGA and in otherwise normal newborn infants who suffered asphyxia or other stress at the time of delivery. A majority of infan

Counter-regulatory hormone deficiencies may be isolated or part of panhypopituitarism. Hypopituitarism should be suspected in children with midline defects (such as cleft lip or cleft palatal), optic nerve hypoplasia and, in males, micropenis. Isolated GH deficiency (GHD) is caused by mutations in the GHRH, GH or their respective receptors. GHD associated with hypopituitarism can be due to central nervous system abnormalities (such as empty sella syndrome, septo-optic dysplasia, pituitary hypoplasia/aplasia) or to acquired causes (such as meningitis, hydrocephalus, radiotherapy, head injury, cerebral infarction, cancer, and surgery). GHD leads to decreased lipolysis and glycogenolysis. Metabolic effects of GHD are represented by ketotic hypoglycemia associated with fasting metabolic acidosis. However, in infants, it presents with a clinical picture identical to that of hyperinsulinism (hypoglycemia associated with low/normal levels of ketone bodies and fatty acids, absence of metabolic acidosis and positive response to glucagon administration). Other clinical features are prolonged and recurrent jaundice in infants, early and progressive growth deceleration during the first years of life, and dysmorphic features with midline defects (in hypopituitarism) occur. The treatment is hormone-replacement therapy; in cases of persistent hypoglycemia, GH treatment can be initiated during the neonatal period with daily subcutaneous injections of recombinant human GH in the evening to mimic the physiological release of GH. Familial chylomicronemia syndrome, characterized by the accumulation of extremely high levels of chylomicrons and in many cases VLDL is the result of inherited deficiencies in key factors in the pathways of TRL assembly and clearance. One of the best characterized of these disorders is absence of functional lipoprotein lipase (LpL) activity in which VLDL catabolism is severely impaired, in particular the lipolysis of VLDL1 (Figure 3). In experiments using tracers of radio-iodinated VLDL1 and VLDL2 in subjects with the condition, it was observed that the FCR of VLDL1 was decreased 10-fold but apoB production into this lipoprotein fraction was similar to normal. VLDL2 clearance, on the other hand, was not significantly impaired by lack of LpL. Deficiency of the other key lipase in lipoprotein metabolism—hepatic lipase (HL)—is associated with hypertriglyceridemia but not to the same extent as seen in LpL deficiency. Investigations reveal that this enzyme is more active at hydrolyzing lipid in smaller particles in the VLDL2, IDL, and LDL density intervals. HL deficient subjects exhibit reduced clearance rates for VLDL and IDL, and slowed conversion of VLDL2 to IDL and IDL to LDL (Figure 3). In the subject we studied there was an almost complete inability to convert IDL to LDL.

Presentation: A 1-year-old Sri Lankan boy was brought to the pediatric service for evaluation and treatment of an upper respiratory tract infection. He was the second child, born at 38 weeks of gestation via normal vaginal delivery after an uneventful pregnancy to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents. His birth and neonatal period were unremarkable, and he was exclusively breastfed. On physical examination, the infant exhibited mild hepatomegaly with a liver palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin. Blood samples taken during the assessment were noted to be grossly lipemic. There were no signs of eruptive xanthomas or epigastric abdominal pain; however, fundoscopy showed lipemia retinalis. His elder sister was in good health. The mother had a history of dyslipidemia diagnosed at 30 years of age and was on lipid-lowering therapy. Liver and renal function tests were normal, as was serum uric acid, but plasma lactate was elevated at 27.3 mg/dL (reference range: 4.5-19.8). A complete blood count revealed mild microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed mild hepatomegaly and moderate splenomegaly.. Confirmed diagnosis: Lipoprotein Lipase Deficiency. Differential diagnosis includes: Lipoprotein Lipase Deficiency.

We have not assessed the impact of APOA5 deficiency on the background of ANGPTL8 deficiency. Because APOA5 functions to suppress ANGPTL3/8 activity, our expectation is that APOA5 deficiency would have little impact on LPL levels in capillaries of heart and brown adipose tissue in Angptl8-deficient mice. Immediately after birth, these infants are at high risk for hypoglycemia but, usually, this condition resolves spontaneously in a few days until the beta-pancreatic cells adapt to the normoglycemic state. In addition, gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is associated with long-term complications for offspring including childhood obesity and glucose intolerance. The molecular basis of offspring adiposity and glucose intolerance is expected to be correlated to genetic and epigenetic modifications owing to intrauterine hyperglycemia. Counter-regulatory hormone deficiencies may be isolated or part of panhypopituitarism. Hypopituitarism should be suspected in children with midline defects (such as cleft lip or cleft palatal), optic nerve hypoplasia and, in males, micropenis. Isolated GH deficiency (GHD) is caused by mutations in the GHRH, GH or their respective receptors. GHD associated with hypopituitarism can be due to central nervous system abnormalities (such as empty sella syndrome, septo-optic dysplasia, pituitary hypoplasia/aplasia) or to acquired causes (such as meningitis, hydrocephalus, radiotherapy, head injury, cerebral infarction, cancer, and surgery). GHD leads to decreased lipolysis and glycogenolysis. Metabolic effects of GHD are represented by ketotic hypoglycemia associated with fasting metabolic acidosis. However, in infants, it presents with a clinical picture identical to that of hyperinsulinism (hypoglycemia associated with low/normal levels of ketone bodies and fatty acids, absence of metabolic acidosis and positive response to glucagon administration). Other clinical features are prolonged and recurrent jaundice in infants, early and progressive growth deceleration during the first years of life, and dysmorphic features with midline defects (in hypopituitarism) occur. The treatment is hormone-replacement therapy; in cases of persistent hypoglycemia, GH treatment can be initiated during the neonatal period with daily subcutaneous injections of recombinant human GH in the evening to mimic the physiological release of GH. Familial chylomicronemia syndrome, characterized by the accumulation of extremely high levels of chylomicrons and in many cases VLDL is the result of inherited deficiencies in key factors in the pathways of TRL assembly and clearance. One of the best characterized of these disorders is absence of functional lipoprotein lipase (LpL) activity in which VLDL catabolism is severely impaired, in particular the lipolysis of VLDL1 (Figure 3). In experiments using tracers of radio-iodinated VLDL1 and VLDL2 in subjects with the condition, it was observed that the FCR of VLDL1 was decreased 10-fold but apoB production into this lipoprotein fraction was similar to normal. VLDL2 clearance, on the other hand, was not significantly impaired by lack of LpL. Deficiency of the other key lipase in lipoprotein metabolism—hepatic lipase (HL)—is associated with hypertriglyceridemia but not to the same extent as seen in LpL deficiency. Investigations reveal that this enzyme is more active at hydrolyzing lipid in smaller particles in the VLDL2, IDL, and LDL density intervals. HL deficient subjects exhibit reduced clearance rates for VLDL and IDL, and slowed conversion of VLDL2 to IDL and IDL to LDL (Figure 3). In the subject we studied there was an almost complete inability to convert IDL to LDL.

Presentation: A 1-year-old Sri Lankan boy was brought to the pediatric service for evaluation and treatment of an upper respiratory tract infection. He was the second child, born at 38 weeks of gestation via normal vaginal delivery after an uneventful pregnancy to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents. His birth and neonatal period were unremarkable, and he was exclusively breastfed. On physical examination, the infant exhibited mild hepatomegaly with a liver palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin. Blood samples taken during the assessment were noted to be grossly lipemic. There were no signs of eruptive xanthomas or epigastric abdominal pain; however, fundoscopy showed lipemia retinalis. His elder sister was in good health. Liver and renal function tests were normal, as was serum uric acid, but plasma lactate was elevated at 27.3 mg/dL (reference range: 4.5-19.8). Vertical SGP (especially downward) is a key feature of Niemann–Pick type C (NPC), present in 65%. NPC is an autosomal-recessive illness caused by mutations in the NPC1 or NPC2 gene, in which cholesterol and lipids accumulate due to a defect in intracellular lipid trafficking. Additional features include gelastic cataplexy and hepatosplenomegaly, although in adult-onset cases, visceromegaly may be absent.

Presentation: A 28-year-old male presented with a history of frequent urination and urgency over an extended period. He was born at full term, and there is no family history of similar symptoms. Physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests, including blood work, renal function, electrolyte levels, and routine urine analysis, all returned normal results.. Confirmed diagnosis: Congenital absence of the sacrum. Differential diagnosis includes: Congenital absence of the sacrum.

Presentation: A 16-day-old female infant presented with bilious vomiting and absence of meconium passage. No antenatal ultrasonography was conducted, and there was no reported maternal drug intake during pregnancy. The baby was delivered at home via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 1.3 kg, and was in a sick and dehydrated state upon admission. Vital signs included a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per minute, a pulse rate of 150 beats per minute, and a blood pressure reading of 80/60 mmHg. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal distention with a soft abdomen and no rigidity. The anal opening was normally positioned. Laboratory results showed a normal haemogram, but serum urea and creatinine levels were moderately elevated.. Confirmed diagnosis: Congenital Absence of Jejunum and Ileum. Differential diagnosis includes: Congenital Absence of Jejunum and Ileum.

A 5-year-old female child is brought to a medical office with complaints of progressive abdominal pain that has intensified in the last 24 hours. The father reports a history of constipation, with no bowel movement for the past 72 hours and no bloody stools. She has experienced three episodes of vomiting since the previous night and is refusing food. Her medical and surgical history is unremarkable. Physical examination reveals upper abdominal distention with tympany, but no abdominal mass, involuntary guarding, or rebound tenderness is detected. What is the most probable underlying etiology of her clinical presentation?

Options:
A. Hirschsprung disease
B. Intestinal lymphoma
C. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome
D. Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction
E. Volvulus
F. Malrotation of the gut
G. Pyloric stenosis
H. Intussusception
I. Meckel diverticulum
J. Duodenal web

knowledge_chunks.text: Presentation: A 26-year-old female (primigravida) underwent an emergency cesarean section at 40 weeks after failed induction. The surgery was completed under spinal anesthesia, and a male neonate was delivered with a birthweight of 3.47 kg and a length of 51 cm. There were no complications during pregnancy, and all prenatal sonographic exams were normal. The newborn examination showed no dysmorphism. Post-C-section, the baby was transferred to the nursery for routine care and feeding. However, 24 hours post-delivery, the baby was moved to the neonatal intensive care unit due to poor feeding, bilious vomiting, and abdominal distension. Physical examination revealed normal vitals, persistent abdominal distension upon palpation, sluggish movements, and bloody mucoid stools. The baby was put under nil by mouth, and a nasogastric tube was inserted, revealing a light greenish aspirate. An x-ray showed multiple loops of dilated small bowel indicating obstruction. Intravenous fluids were started, and antibiotics (amoxicillin 50 mg every 12 hours and gentamicin 5 mg every 48 hours) were administered due to the possibility of bowel necrosis and perforation. The case was referred to pediatric surgery, and . Confirmed diagnosis: Hirschsprung’s disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Hirschsprung’s disease.

Entamoeba hiatolytica, which causes amoebic colitis, is another IBD mimicker that can cause bloody diarrhea. Endoscopic findings include skip lesions and multifocal ulceration, which is more common on the right side of the colon and can mimic CD. Microbiologically, the diagnosis of amoebiasis can be made by stool microscopy and periodic‐acid Schiff (PAS) positive trophozoites on biopsy. Histologically, there are flask‐shaped ulcers with florid necroinflammatory exudate, erythrophagocytosis, cryptitis, lamina propria‐containing chronic inflammatory infiltrates, surface epithelial damage, and PAS stains highlight the organisms. In contrast to IBD, the mucosa adjacent to the amoebic ulcers is normal, with an absence of granuloma. Of note, chronic amoebic infection can lead to crypt distortion and fibrosis, which could mimic IBD.

Presentation: Patient A, a 31-year-old woman, visited the hospital on 1 June 2017 due to 'fatigue and dizziness for 1 month and worsening for 1 week.' The patient experienced dizziness and fatigue without any clear cause 1 month prior, with symptoms intensifying over the past week. She sought care at the emergency department. Blood tests revealed a hemoglobin (HGB) level of 38 g/L, and esophagogastroduodenoscopy indicated chronic superficial gastritis. Despite blood replenishment treatment, severe anemia persisted, and symptoms of dizziness and fatigue showed minimal improvement. Consequently, the patient was admitted for 'anemia of unknown origin.' During her hospital stay, she did not report nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, abdominal distension, black stool, or bloody stool. Physical examination noted an anemic appearance, a soft abdomen without tenderness or rebound pain, no palpable masses, and bowel sounds occurring six times per minute. Admission findings included anemia of unknown origin. Blood tests showed HGB at 45 g/L; urine analysis revealed 94 RBC/μl; stool occult blood test was positive; and tumor marker tests indicated erythropoietin levels >762.00 mIU/ml. Contrast-enhanced CT sca. Confirmed diagnosis: Small Intestinal Lymphangioma. Differential diagnosis includes: Small Intestinal Lymphangioma.

Presentation: A 38-year-old male with a history of type III intestinal failure due to chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction related to gastrointestinal dysmotility, cardiac and intestinal arrhythmia syndrome, dependence on parenteral nutrition, sinus dysfunction, and a pacemaker. The patient has chronic intestinal insufficiency due to a motor disorder of the intestines and has been part of an intestinal rehabilitation program requiring regular monitoring of nutritional, biometric, and electrolytic parameters. The patient was admitted to a high-complexity hospital presenting with diffuse, mild-intensity abdominal pain for six days and multiple vomiting episodes. There was no fever, diarrhea, jaundice, or other associated symptoms. Vital signs upon admission were: blood pressure 98/54 mmHg, heart rate 67 per minute, respiratory rate 16 per minute, and oxygen saturation 95%. Physical examination showed an alert and oriented patient with mild dehydration, minimal tenderness upon abdominal palpation, and no clear signs of peritoneal irritation. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed intestinal obstruction with a transition zone in the jejunum, without signs of complications or intestinal loop. Confirmed diagnosis: Wernicke's Encephalopathy. Differential diagnosis includes: Wernicke's Encephalopathy.

knowledge_chunks.text: Presentation: A 26-year-old female (primigravida) underwent an emergency cesarean section at 40 weeks after failed induction. The surgery was completed under spinal anesthesia, and a male neonate was delivered with a birthweight of 3.47 kg and a length of 51 cm. There were no complications during pregnancy, and all prenatal sonographic exams were normal. The newborn examination showed no dysmorphism. Post-C-section, the baby was transferred to the nursery for routine care and feeding. However, 24 hours post-delivery, the baby was moved to the neonatal intensive care unit due to poor feeding, bilious vomiting, and abdominal distension. Physical examination revealed normal vitals, persistent abdominal distension upon palpation, sluggish movements, and bloody mucoid stools. The baby was put under nil by mouth, and a nasogastric tube was inserted, revealing a light greenish aspirate. An x-ray showed multiple loops of dilated small bowel indicating obstruction. Intravenous fluids were started, and antibiotics (amoxicillin 50 mg every 12 hours and gentamicin 5 mg every 48 hours) were administered due to the possibility of bowel necrosis and perforation. The case was referred to pediatric surgery, and . Confirmed diagnosis: Hirschsprung’s disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Hirschsprung’s disease.

Entamoeba hiatolytica, which causes amoebic colitis, is another IBD mimicker that can cause bloody diarrhea. Endoscopic findings include skip lesions and multifocal ulceration, which is more common on the right side of the colon and can mimic CD. Microbiologically, the diagnosis of amoebiasis can be made by stool microscopy and periodic‐acid Schiff (PAS) positive trophozoites on biopsy. Histologically, there are flask‐shaped ulcers with florid necroinflammatory exudate, erythrophagocytosis, cryptitis, lamina propria‐containing chronic inflammatory infiltrates, surface epithelial damage, and PAS stains highlight the organisms. In contrast to IBD, the mucosa adjacent to the amoebic ulcers is normal, with an absence of granuloma. Of note, chronic amoebic infection can lead to crypt distortion and fibrosis, which could mimic IBD.

The diagnostic criteria for CdLS were published by the Medical Director of the CdLS Foundation (Kline et al. ), categorizing the CdLS phenotype into cardinal and suggestive features. Cardinal features, each assigned a score of 2 if present, include synophrys/thick eyebrows, short nose/concave nasal ridge/upturned nasal tip, long/smooth philtrum, thin upper lip vermilion/downturned corners of mouth, hand oligodactyly/adactyly, and ongenital diaphragmatic hernia. Suggestive features are assigned a score of 1 each if present and include global developmental delay/intellectual disability, prenatal growth retardation < 2SD, postnatal growth retardation < 2SD, prenatally/postnatally microcephaly, small hands/ft, short fifth finger, and hirsutism. Individuals with a score of ≥ 11 and at least 3 cardinal features are classified as having classic CdLS. Those with a score of 9–10 and at least 2 cardinal features are classified as having non‐classic CdLS. A score of 4–8 with at least 1 cardinal feature warrants molecular testing for CdLS, whereas a score of < 4 is insufficient to indicate the need for such testing.

Presentation: A 13-year-old male was referred to our department with chest pain, chest deformity, and myopia. The chest pain had been occurring for 5 years, lasting approximately 5 minutes each time. There were no associated palpitations, autonomic symptoms, presyncope or syncope, and the pain was not related to respiration or food intake. Family history revealed that the patient's maternal great-uncles were tall and thin. On physical examination, the patient appeared comfortable at rest, was tall (1.75 m, 97th percentile), and thin with features including long fingers and toes (arachnodactyly), sunken chest (pectus excavatum), long limbs (dolichostenomelia), positive wrist and thumb signs, increased arm span relative to height, elongated head (dolichocephaly), spinal curvature (scoliosis), downward-slanting eye openings (downslanting palpebral fissures), underdeveloped cheekbones (malar hypoplasia), and keloid formation. His total systemic score was 8 based on specific criteria. Laboratory tests, including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, calcium, magnesium and phosphate, and liver function tests, were within normal limits.. Confirmed diagnosis: Marfan syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Marfan syndrome.

Case 2 A third pregnancy was spontaneously conceived some years later. The first trimester scan was normal, with a nuchal translucency of 1.2 mm and a low risk for major aneuploidies at combined test. At 16 weeks, fetal biometry and anatomy were normal. The couple was referred to our hospital at 21 weeks because of the recurrence of FGR. At ultrasound examination FGR was confirmed and multiple morphological abnormalities, similar to those of the first deceased baby, were reported: the hands were clenched during the whole time of the examination with abducted fingers (Fig. 1a); there was a right rocker-bottom foot with plantar edema (Fig. 1b); both superior and inferior limbs were constantly extended with no evidence of flexion-extension at joints; the lenses were bilaterally hyperechoic, suggestive for cataract, and the orbital diameter was bilaterally below the 5th centile (Fig. 1c); slight retrognathia and low implantation of the ears were also reported (Fig. 1d). A multidisciplinary counselling was performed during which the parents were informed regarding the poor prognosis; the likelihood of a hereditary condition and the possibility of a COFS syndrome were hypothesized. The amniocentesis was performed. As first-tier genetic test, we performed a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP’s) array analysis (ILLUMINA Express Exome arrays) and metabolic investigations, including the measurement of 7-dehydrocholesterol, in order to detect any chromosomal molecular abnormality and to exclude the Smith–Lemli–Opitz Syndrome (SLOS).

Next-generation sequencing (NGS) effectively identifies novel gene mutations and discrete genomic variations, hence increasing the genetic diagnostic yield of GDD/ID. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) can be used concurrently to interpret the DNA sequences of thousands of protein-encoding genes using NGS techniques. WES is proven helpful in patients with multiple genetic conditions, atypical presentations of a genetic disorder, and early presentations of a disease for which classic findings are lacking. However, WES has important limitations, one of which is incomplete exome coverage, which does not allow for the examination of all exons potentially affecting the test yield. Moreover, WES does not reliably detect mosaic variants, repetitive sequences, exon-level deletions, epigenetic variants, or balanced rearrangements. In a recent meta-analysis focusing on isolated NDDs, the estimated diagnostic yield of WES was 31%, greater than that of CMA (15%). Higher yields were observed in patients with abnormal head size, younger age at presentation, and developmental epileptic encephalopathy. According to the 2021 American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics guidelines, WES is highly recommended as a first- or second-line test for children with GDD/ID.

Two CMA platforms were used to analyze chromosome array comparative genomic hybridization and single-nucleotide variant arrays. Stature is a multifactorial phenotypic trait influenced by multiple genetic and environmental factors. The genetic component is vast, as about 420 genetic loci contribute to adult stature, by encoding mainly proteins expressed in the EGP. Some single gene defects can result in severe growth disorders, while most mutations or polymorphisms in various genetic loci cause low normal stature or idiopathic short stature. This observation highlights the fact that some of the genes involved play a crucial role in human growth, while others play a minor role. In addition, sequence variants in the same genetic locus can be expressed as different clinical entities. The phenotypic manifestation is the net result of the gene involved and the type of mutation in the gene (gain of function, altered function, impaired function or complete loss of function). Therefore, extreme tall stature, low normal stature, idiopathic short stature, and short stature are different phenotypic manifestations of the same clinical spectrum of disorders labelled under the term stature abnormalities (Figure 1). This approach to stature abnormalities has dictated the classification of short stature proposed by the European Society for Pediatric Endocrinology based on the causes of short stature into primary (of genetic origin) and secondary (of endocrine or other origin). This classification is less centred around pathophysiology and constitutes a more useful approach for clinical purposes.

A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for a routine well-child checkup. He began walking at 20 months of age. He is able to drink from a cup but cannot use silverware. He speaks in 2-word phrases and can stack 4 blocks. He can scribble but is unable to draw a circle. His height is above the 99th percentile, and his weight is at the 15th percentile. B. Procollagen peptidase deficiency
C. Type I collagen mutation
D. Deficiency of pyridoxine-dependent enzymes
E. Alpha-1,4-glucosidase deficiency
F. Mutation in the FGFR3 gene
G. Type V collagen deficiency
H. Lysyl hydroxylase deficiency
I. Homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency
J. Cystathionine synthase deficiency

A 33-year-old male construction worker is brought to the emergency department with acute confusion after being found unconscious at his worksite. His medical history includes seizure disorder and schizophrenia, for which he takes haloperidol. He underwent an appendectomy two months ago. On examination, his vital signs show: temperature 105°F (40.6°C), blood pressure 120/84 mmHg, heart rate 150/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The patient is confused and non-communicative, with sweat-soaked clothing. While he shows no clear focal neurologic deficits, he lacks purposeful movement of his extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Anticholinergic toxicity
B. Exertional heat stroke
C. Malignant hyperthermia
D. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
E. Central nervous system infection
F. Drug-induced hyperthermia
G. Septic shock
H. Nonexertional heat stroke
I. Thyroid storm
J. Status epilepticus

On examination, his vital signs show: temperature 105°F (40.6°C), blood pressure 120/84 mmHg, heart rate 150/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The patient is confused and non-communicative, with sweat-soaked clothing. While he shows no clear focal neurologic deficits, he lacks purposeful movement of his extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Anticholinergic toxicity
B. Exertional heat stroke
C. Malignant hyperthermia
D. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
E. Central nervous system infection
F. Drug-induced hyperthermia
G. Septic shock
H. Nonexertional heat stroke
I. Thyroid storm
J. Status epilepticus
