UUI is diagnosed by history and ensuring no acute cystitis, a normal post-void residual and normal screening urinalysis. Urodynamic testing may be considered if there are new-onset urinary symptoms and concern for pelvic nerve injury, such as in the setting of a prolonged second stage of labor or operative vaginal delivery. In women who have suspected bladder overdistension injury, urodynamics could help with diagnosis and determining prognosis, however, they are not mandatory.

Presentation: An 83-year-old man with a history of hypertension and asthma, and no prior abdominal surgeries, presented to the Department of General Surgery with an 8 × 8 cm necrotic area at the scrotal base. Nineteen years earlier, the patient had received radiation therapy twice over four years, totaling 82 Gy, for a condition in the same region. The patient was evaluated by colorectal surgeons, plastic surgeons, and urologists. The lesion was located at the scrotal base and featured a necrotic ulcer in the perianal area. Initial assessments considered the condition as a potential side effect of previous radiation therapy. Multiple biopsies were performed, and histopathological examination revealed specific findings without signs of invasiveness. Further clinical workup, including a normal colonoscopy and MRI of the lower abdomen, ruled out involvement of the urethra or corpora cavernosum.. Confirmed diagnosis: Primary perianal Paget’s disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Primary perianal Paget’s disease.

Presentation: A 42-year-old male with a history of cervical spine injury resulting in paraplegia since adolescence and end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, as well as a small bowel obstruction treated with lysis of adhesions six months prior, presented with chronic abdominal pain and progressive abdominal distension over three months. His vital signs were stable and he was afebrile. Physical examination revealed a markedly tense abdomen with generalized tenderness and dullness on percussion. No signs of chronic liver disease were noted. Given his history of small bowel obstruction and the severity of his pain, a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. The CT scan showed no obstruction or perforation but revealed a large amount of loculated ascites, multiple adhesions with small bowel loops tethered to these adhesions, and hepatomegaly without evidence of cirrhosis or biliary tract obstruction. Confirmed diagnosis: Hepatic transthyretin amyloidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Hepatic transthyretin amyloidosis.

Presentation: A 48-year-old male was admitted to Beijing YouAn Hospital with liver cirrhosis. Four months prior, an abdominal ultrasound indicated cirrhosis and splenomegaly, despite the patient experiencing no discomfort. At another hospital, he was diagnosed with diabetes and started on insulin therapy. The patient reported minimal alcohol consumption and no family history of liver diseases. Physical examination revealed skin pigmentation but no other abnormalities. Liver function tests showed elevated levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST). Serum markers for viral hepatitis and autoimmune liver diseases were negative. Plasma iron indices were abnormal: iron at 47 μmol/L, transferrin saturation at 97.9%, and ferritin levels exceeding 2000 ng/ml. HbA1c was significantly elevated, while testosterone levels were normal at 18.26 nmol/L. Pre-contrast computed tomography (CT) showed hepatomegaly with increased attenuation in the liver and spleen, splenomegaly, and formation of collateral circulation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a typical decrease in T2-weighted signal intensity over the liver.. Confirmed diagnosis: Type 3 Hemochromatosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Type 3 Hemochromatosis.

Presentation: A 55-year-old Caucasian male with a history of multiple myeloma currently undergoing chemotherapy with Velcade, Cytoxan, and dexamethasone, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, atrial flutter post-ablation, and melanoma of the left thigh post-surgical resection with negative lymph nodes and in remission, presented to the hospital with multiple episodes of nausea and vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain, subjective fevers, and chills over the past 2 days. His last bowel movement was 2 days ago. On presentation, his vitals were stable. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel, were normal. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast showed a partial small bowel obstruction. A small bowel follow-through indicated non-specific thickening of the proximal small bowel loops. This was his third hospitalization with the same presentation of small bowel obstruction, with previous admissions one month ago and 2 weeks ago. During the initial hospitalization, an exploratory laparotomy showed no findings to suggest mechanical small bowel obstruction. An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with push enteroscopy identified enteritis and a Mallory-Weis. Confirmed diagnosis: Gastrointestinal Amyloidosis. Differential diagnosis includes: Gastrointestinal Amyloidosis.

Presentation: A three-day-old newborn male presented to the emergency department with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting starting on the second day after birth. Direct abdominal radiography and abdominal ultrasound did not reveal any abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests and thyroid hormone levels were within normal limits. A contrast enema radiography was conducted to investigate neonatal congenital bowel issues, but no abnormalities were detected. The patient resumed normal oral feeding for two days, after which vomiting recurred. Nasogastric intubation produced drainage containing fecalith, and there was an increase in abdominal distension, leading to the decision for an emergency operation.. Confirmed diagnosis: Ileum Duplication Cyst. Differential diagnosis includes: Ileum Duplication Cyst.

A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with nausea and vomiting for the past week. He decided to come in when his symptoms worsened. He feels that his symptoms are exacerbated with large fatty meals and when he drinks alcohol. His wife recently returned from a cruise with symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea. The patient has a medical history of poorly managed diabetes, constipation, anxiety, dyslipidemia, and hypertension. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 197/128 mmHg, pulse is 100/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Physical exam reveals a systolic murmur heard loudest along the left upper sternal border. Abdominal exam reveals an obese, tympanitic and distended abdomen with a 3 cm scar in the right lower quadrant. Vascular exam reveals weak pulses in the lower extremities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying etiology of this patient's symptoms?

Options:
A. Adhesions
B. Enteric nervous system damage
C. Impacted stool
D. Norovirus
E. Twisting of the bowel

Studies have shown that sleep quality in young adults and middle-aged patients was heavily influenced by the surgical start time. Patients with surgeries that occurred in the afternoon (14:00–18:00) had increased levels of cortisol and decreased melatonin on postoperative night one than patients who underwent surgery in the morning, resulting in the afternoon group having almost twice the rate of sleep disturbances (70% of patients vs. 39%, respectively). Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is a condition where excessive amounts of bacteria typically found in the colon are found in the small intestine and result in various gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms. Patient with IBD, particularly Crohn’s disease, are at increased risk of SIBO. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the proportion of SIBO in patients with IBD was 22.3% (95% CI 19.92–24.68). The odds ratio (OR) for SIBO in patients with IBD was 9.51 (95% CI 3.39–26.68) compared to controls without IBD. The OR was significantly elevated in both CD (OR 10.86; 95% CI 2.76–42.69) and UC (OR 7.96; 95% CI 1.66–38.35). In subgroup analysis, patients with fibrostenosing CD (OR 7.47; 95% CI 2.51–22.20) and prior bowel surgery (OR 2.38; 95% CI 1.65–3.44), had increased odds of SIBO. The underlying pathophysiology behind SIBO in IBD may be due to impaired intestinal mucosal integrity, intestinal stasis caused by strictures, and/or intra-abdominal adhesions and prior intestinal surgeries. Additionally, any structural factor that allows colonic bacteria to enter the small bowel, such as enterocolic fistulas or lack of an ileocecal valve can facilitate SIBO. The symptoms of SIBO are non-specific and non-predictive for SIBO, however commonly patients complain of bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, nausea, dyspepsia, diarrhea, and constipation. The preferred method to diagnose SIBO is the lactulose or glucose breath test (Table 1). The test is considered positive if there is a rise in baseline breath hydrogen by ≥ 20 by 90 min. knowledge_chunks.text: The search process used the following terms ‘c-section’, ‘C-Sections’, ‘Cesarean’, ‘Adhesions’, ‘Surgery Induced Tissue Adhesions’ and ‘sliding sign’. Studies were considered for eligibility if the population was gravida women with at least 1 prior CD, the diagnostic test was the absence of sliding sign in trans-abdominal ultrasonography, the reference test was surgical reports following CD and the outcome was existence of intra-abdominal adhesions involving the uterus. Intraabdominal adhesions in included studies involved any adhesions related to the access of the surgeons to the planned uterine incision (thin, filmy and easily separated adhesions by gentle, blunt or manual dissection with no vascular structures or adhesions between bowel or bladder and anterior uterine side making access to the lower uterine segment difficult and often require sharp dissection to release). Based on intraoperative findings, 4 levels of adhesions were identified: absent, mild (little or filmy adhesions), moderate (moderate to thick adhesions, require sharp dissection but do not involve bladder or bowel), and severe (absence of free space between uterine and abdominal walls or adhesions between uterus and bladder or bowel). A freely moving uterus indicated a low chance of adhesions (positive sliding sign). No uterine movement under the fascia of abdominal muscles suggested severe adhesions (negative sliding sign). US findings were compared to surgical reports following CD surgery as the reference standard test.

Lung CT scan has been used to understand the pathophysiology and the interplay with mechanical ventilation. CT scan clearly showed that ARDS is a non-homogeneous lung disease with the following classically reported morphological patterns: consolidated regions (defined by a homogenous increase in density without vessels or bronchi), ground glass areas (with an increase in density with still recognizable vessels) and the normal aerated regions. These three morphological features are usually simultaneously present. Air bronchograms and small pleural effusions are also common. The dependent localization of consolidated areas is related to the increase in lung oedema (i.e. increase in lung weight) during the initial phase of ARDS which raises the hydrostatic pressure transmitted throughout the lung, causing a reduction in lung gas volume and the development of non-aerated lung regions. These poorly or non-aerated lung regions are characterized by a higher inflammation than normally ventilated lung regions. The presence of non-inflated areas causes a major expansion of the neighbouring lung regions and generation of higher local pressures which act as a “stress raiser”. Higher amounts of inhomogeneities are accompanied by higher stress raisers and severity of ARDS and worse outcome. Pulmonary ARDS presents a similar amount of consolidated and ground glass areas while extrapulmonary ARDS has a higher amount of ground glass areas. The timing and type of surgery have also been observed to play a role in developing PSD. Studies have shown that sleep quality in young adults and middle-aged patients was heavily influenced by the surgical start time. Patients with surgeries that occurred in the afternoon (14:00–18:00) had increased levels of cortisol and decreased melatonin on postoperative night one than patients who underwent surgery in the morning, resulting in the afternoon group having almost twice the rate of sleep disturbances (70% of patients vs. 39%, respectively). It is believed that patients with morning surgeries may achieve better sleep due to having a recovery period that does not overlap with a sleeping period. Interestingly, these results were not observed in older patients, presumably due to their decreased metabolism, which requires longer periods of time to recover from surgery. With regards to how the type of surgery affects the development of PSDs, major surgery has been found to have a greater suppressive effect on slow wave sleep and REM sleep than minor surgery. Gögenur et al. found that sleep quality after laparoscopic surgery returned to normal values in under a week compared to major abdominal surgery sleep recovery, which took over 4 weeks. This is believed to be related to the increased levels of trauma that occur in major abdominal surgery. Additionally, major abdominal surgery usually necessitates longer hospital stays, while laparoscopic patients may be discharged from the hospital on the same day. Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is a condition where excessive amounts of bacteria typically found in the colon are found in the small intestine and result in various gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms. Patient with IBD, particularly Crohn’s disease, are at increased risk of SIBO. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, the proportion of SIBO in patients with IBD was 22.3% (95% CI 19.92–24.68). The odds ratio (OR) for SIBO in patients with IBD was 9.51 (95% CI 3.39–26.68) compared to controls without IBD. The OR was significantly elevated in both CD (OR 10.86; 95% CI 2.76–42.69) and UC (OR 7.96; 95% CI 1.66–38.35). In subgroup analysis, patients with fibrostenosing CD (OR 7.47; 95% CI 2.51–22.20) and prior bowel surgery (OR 2.38; 95% CI 1.65–3.44), had increased odds of SIBO. The underlying pathophysiology behind SIBO in IBD may be due to impaired intestinal mucosal integrity, intestinal stasis caused by strictures, and/or intra-abdominal adhesions and prior intestinal surgeries. Additionally, any structural factor that allows colonic bacteria to enter the small bowel, such as enterocolic fistulas or lack of an ileocecal valve can facilitate SIBO. The symptoms of SIBO are non-specific and non-predictive for SIBO, however commonly patients complain of bloating, abdominal pain, flatulence, nausea, dyspepsia, diarrhea, and constipation. The preferred method to diagnose SIBO is the lactulose or glucose breath test (Table 1). The test is considered positive if there is a rise in baseline breath hydrogen by ≥ 20 by 90 min. Diagnosing SUI based on classic symptoms can be easily confirmed during pelvic examination, by asking the patient to cough or Valsalva with a full bladder. If the provider observes urine leaking from the urethra during an office cough/Valsalva stress test, the diagnosis of SUI is confirmed. Urodynamic testing can also be performed to confirm a suspected diagnosis of SUI, however, based on the Value of Urodynamic Evaluation study, in women with uncomplicated SUI without significant prolapse or urinary urgency, if SUI is demonstrated on examination, additional urodynamic testing is not necessary before treatment. UUI is diagnosed by history and ensuring no acute cystitis, a normal post-void residual and normal screening urinalysis. Urodynamic testing may be considered if there are new-onset urinary symptoms and concern for pelvic nerve injury, such as in the setting of a prolonged second stage of labor or operative vaginal delivery. In women who have suspected bladder overdistension injury, urodynamics could help with diagnosis and determining prognosis, however, they are not mandatory.

knowledge_chunks.text: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.

As respiratory pediatricians we all experienced that low-dose inhaled corticosteroids can easily control asthma symptoms in most of patients. Moreover, exacerbations in children are often concentrated in some periods of the year due to viral trigger or aeroallergens, and some little patients can even stop their treatment in summer time without clinical deterioration. Nevertheless, children and their parents sometimes keep complaining of recurrent respiratory symptoms despite the correct and continuous treatment, and various courses of antibiotics, beta-2 agonists and oral corticosteroids are frequently prescribed by pediatrician. As a consequence of the poor symptoms control, asthma treatment is often increased and the patient categorized as “problematic severe asthmatic.” However, an earlier step could be identified and this condition better defined as “problematic respiratory symptoms unresponsive to prescribed asthma therapy”. In fact, the known expression: “Not all that wheezes is asthma” continues to be relevant and the asthma diagnosis should be clinically reconsidered. In the last few decades, we possibly moved from under diagnosing to over diagnosing asthma. Nowadays, a thriving child with history of recurrent cough and a need of frequent beta-2 and inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) treatment is often diagnosed with “probable asthma” and ICS in ever increasing doses immediately prescribed. A hair visible in the skin ostium is considered to be pathognomonic for ND (Figure 1). NDs may be noticeable at birth, presenting as a lump or a pit on the nasal dorsum. The majority of them are diagnosed at infancy or in early childhood, but there are some reports of later diagnoses. A slow-growing mass may be observed in some cases in early infancy. Half of children may present hypertelorism and a broadened nasal bridge. Palpation may reveal a subcutaneous mass in 30% of patients, typically at the level of the osteocartilaginuous junction. Some authors have reported intracranial epidermoid and dermoid cysts in the proximity of the crista galli or foramen caecum without typical nasal manifestation. Intermittent sebaceous discharge from the skin ostium may be observed. Multiple ostia and cysts at more than one level are a rarity. The presence of a sinus opening increases the risk of infection and further complications. The probability of infection is estimated to be 7% per year throughout childhood. Presentation: A 29-year-old woman experienced recurrent bilateral purulent nasal discharge for 3 months. The symptoms began 3 months prior, accompanied by dizziness and headache. She had a cesarean birth at a local hospital 4 years ago and has no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed slightly congested mucosa in the bilateral nasal cavity, slightly enlarged inferior turbinates, hypertrophic middle turbinates, and a small amount of purulent nasal discharge in both middle nasal passages and posterior nostrils. Laboratory tests indicated slightly elevated serum uric acid (428.9 μmol/L), fibrin (4.9 g/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (30 mm/h), and ultrasensitive thyroid stimulating hormone (5.1 μIU/mL) levels, while myoglobin (< 21 ng/mL) was slightly decreased. Complete blood count, electrolyte profiles, and liver function were normal. A computed tomography scan from another hospital showed bilateral maxillary sinusitis, ethmoiditis, and bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy. A preoperative noncontrast chest computed tomography scan revealed a high-riding, tortuous structure extending to the mid-upper level of the first thoracic vertebra with local cystic dilatation, and a fe. Confirmed diagnosis: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery. Differential diagnosis includes: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery.

Asthma diagnosis is often suspected when a constellation of typical features is present, however, as most guidelines highlight, diagnosis has to be confirmed either by objective tests or an objective response to treatment. One of the initial major error that occurs is that insufficient features of the asthma pattern are sought before the diagnosis is made. Patient's history should always give enough answers to the following question: “Does the child have any or all of cough, wheeze and breathlessness?.” A persistent cough (especially if non-productive) alone in an otherwise well-child is highly unlikely be due to asthma. payload.vignette:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents for worsening symptoms of previously diagnosed acute sinusitis. Initially, the pediatrician prescribed decongestants and sent the patient home. Since then, the patient has developed a nasal discharge with worsening pain. The patient has a medical history of asthma which is well-controlled with albuterol. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 90/48 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Inspection of the patient's nose reveals a unilateral purulent discharge mixed with blood. The rest of the patient's exam is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Bleeding and infected vessel of Kiesselbach plexus
B. Foreign body obstruction
C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
D. Septal perforation
E. Sinusitis with bacterial superinfection

knowledge_chunks.text: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.

As respiratory pediatricians we all experienced that low-dose inhaled corticosteroids can easily control asthma symptoms in most of patients. Moreover, exacerbations in children are often concentrated in some periods of the year due to viral trigger or aeroallergens, and some little patients can even stop their treatment in summer time without clinical deterioration. Nevertheless, children and their parents sometimes keep complaining of recurrent respiratory symptoms despite the correct and continuous treatment, and various courses of antibiotics, beta-2 agonists and oral corticosteroids are frequently prescribed by pediatrician. As a consequence of the poor symptoms control, asthma treatment is often increased and the patient categorized as “problematic severe asthmatic.” However, an earlier step could be identified and this condition better defined as “problematic respiratory symptoms unresponsive to prescribed asthma therapy”. In fact, the known expression: “Not all that wheezes is asthma” continues to be relevant and the asthma diagnosis should be clinically reconsidered. In the last few decades, we possibly moved from under diagnosing to over diagnosing asthma. Nowadays, a thriving child with history of recurrent cough and a need of frequent beta-2 and inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) treatment is often diagnosed with “probable asthma” and ICS in ever increasing doses immediately prescribed. The initial suspected diagnosis, made with insufficient features and no spirometry testing, gradually, and with no evidence, becomes a definitive diagnosis rarely questioned in the fut

NDs may present as a cyst, sinus, or fistula located anywhere from the philtrum of the upper lip to the glabellar region. A hair visible in the skin ostium is considered to be pathognomonic for ND (Figure 1). NDs may be noticeable at birth, presenting as a lump or a pit on the nasal dorsum. The majority of them are diagnosed at infancy or in early childhood, but there are some reports of later diagnoses. A slow-growing mass may be observed in some cases in early infancy. Half of children may present hypertelorism and a broadened nasal bridge. Palpation may reveal a subcutaneous mass in 30% of patients, typically at the level of the osteocartilaginuous junction. Some authors have reported intracranial epidermoid and dermoid cysts in the proximity of the crista galli or foramen caecum without typical nasal manifestation. Intermittent sebaceous discharge from the skin ostium may be observed. Multiple ostia and cysts at more than one level are a rarity. The presence of a sinus opening increases the risk of infection and further complications. The probability of infection is estimated to be 7% per year throughout childhood. Owusu-Aim et al. revealed that 50% of children have at least one local infection by the age of 4, and more than 90% before their 9th birthday. Recurring infections influence the long-term results of surgical treatment. Intracranial involvement is estimated in 20% of cases but ranges from 4% to 57% in different studies, and it is impossible to determine clinically as there is no correlation between the location of the sinus ostium or cyst and the presence of a

Presentation: A 29-year-old woman experienced recurrent bilateral purulent nasal discharge for 3 months. The symptoms began 3 months prior, accompanied by dizziness and headache. She had a cesarean birth at a local hospital 4 years ago and has no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed slightly congested mucosa in the bilateral nasal cavity, slightly enlarged inferior turbinates, hypertrophic middle turbinates, and a small amount of purulent nasal discharge in both middle nasal passages and posterior nostrils. Laboratory tests indicated slightly elevated serum uric acid (428.9 μmol/L), fibrin (4.9 g/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (30 mm/h), and ultrasensitive thyroid stimulating hormone (5.1 μIU/mL) levels, while myoglobin (< 21 ng/mL) was slightly decreased. Complete blood count, electrolyte profiles, and liver function were normal. A computed tomography scan from another hospital showed bilateral maxillary sinusitis, ethmoiditis, and bilateral inferior turbinate hypertrophy. A preoperative noncontrast chest computed tomography scan revealed a high-riding, tortuous structure extending to the mid-upper level of the first thoracic vertebra with local cystic dilatation, and a fe. Confirmed diagnosis: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery. Differential diagnosis includes: Cervical aortic arch with aneurysm formation and an anomalous right subclavian artery and left vertebral artery.

A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents for worsening symptoms of previously diagnosed acute sinusitis. Initially, the pediatrician prescribed decongestants and sent the patient home. Since then, the patient has developed a nasal discharge with worsening pain. The patient has a medical history of asthma which is well-controlled with albuterol. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 90/48 mmHg, pulse is 124/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The cardiopulmonary exam is within normal limits. Inspection of the patient's nose reveals a unilateral purulent discharge mixed with blood. The rest of the patient's exam is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Bleeding and infected vessel of Kiesselbach plexus
B. Foreign body obstruction
C. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
D. Septal perforation
E. Sinusitis with bacterial superinfection

knowledge_chunks.text: Both adult and child migraineurs are frequently misdiagnosed as having “sinus headaches”. In one adult study, 35% of the migraineurs had undergone previous sinus surgery. This was demonstrated by an observational study that included 3000 individuals with a history of self- or clinician-diagnosed “sinus headaches”, in which 88% of these patients met the diagnostic criteria for migraine. However, most of these patients reported additional typical migraine symptoms, such as photophobia, phonophobia, and pulsating head pain. Migraine can be mistaken for sinus headache because of the similarity in location of the headache and the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms. Pain due to pathology of the nasal mucosa or related structures is usually perceived as frontal or facial, but may be referred more posteriorly, making a proper diagnosis difficult. The presence of purulent nasal discharge and the character of the pain, which is typically pressure-like and reproduced by palpation over the sinuses, help to differentiate these two conditions.

As respiratory pediatricians we all experienced that low-dose inhaled corticosteroids can easily control asthma symptoms in most of patients. Moreover, exacerbations in children are often concentrated in some periods of the year due to viral trigger or aeroallergens, and some little patients can even stop their treatment in summer time without clinical deterioration. Nevertheless, children and their parents sometimes keep complaining of recurrent respiratory symptoms despite the correct and continuous treatment, and various courses of antibiotics, beta-2 agonists and oral corticosteroids are frequently prescribed by pediatrician. As a consequence of the poor symptoms control, asthma treatment is often increased and the patient categorized as “problematic severe asthmatic.” However, an earlier step could be identified and this condition better defined as “problematic respiratory symptoms unresponsive to prescribed asthma therapy”. In fact, the known expression: “Not all that wheezes is asthma” continues to be relevant and the asthma diagnosis should be clinically reconsidered. In the last few decades, we possibly moved from under diagnosing to over diagnosing asthma. Nowadays, a thriving child with history of recurrent cough and a need of frequent beta-2 and inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) treatment is often diagnosed with “probable asthma” and ICS in ever increasing doses immediately prescribed. The initial suspected diagnosis, made with insufficient features and no spirometry testing, gradually, and with no evidence, becomes a definitive diagnosis rarely questioned in the fut

NDs may present as a cyst, sinus, or fistula located anywhere from the philtrum of the upper lip to the glabellar region. A hair visible in the skin ostium is considered to be pathognomonic for ND (Figure 1). NDs may be noticeable at birth, presenting as a lump or a pit on the nasal dorsum. The majority of them are diagnosed at infancy or in early childhood, but there are some reports of later diagnoses. A slow-growing mass may be observed in some cases in early infancy. Half of children may present hypertelorism and a broadened nasal bridge. Palpation may reveal a subcutaneous mass in 30% of patients, typically at the level of the osteocartilaginuous junction. Some authors have reported intracranial epidermoid and dermoid cysts in the proximity of the crista galli or foramen caecum without typical nasal manifestation. Intermittent sebaceous discharge from the skin ostium may be observed. Multiple ostia and cysts at more than one level are a rarity. The presence of a sinus opening increases the risk of infection and further complications. The probability of infection is estimated to be 7% per year throughout childhood. Owusu-Aim et al. revealed that 50% of children have at least one local infection by the age of 4, and more than 90% before their 9th birthday. Recurring infections influence the long-term results of surgical treatment. Intracranial involvement is estimated in 20% of cases but ranges from 4% to 57% in different studies, and it is impossible to determine clinically as there is no correlation between the location of the sinus ostium or cyst and the presence of a

A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with complaints of a sore throat and difficulty breathing. His mother reports that the symptoms began the previous night and have worsened rapidly. The child is normally healthy, up to date on all childhood vaccinations, and takes a daily multivitamin. His temperature is 103°F (39.4°C), blood pressure is 100/64 mmHg, pulse is 155/min, respirations are 29/min, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. On examination, he appears ill, is drooling, and leans forward to breathe. He is nonverbal, visibly uncomfortable, and does not cooperate with an oral examination. What is the most likely infectious cause of this patient’s symptoms?

Options:
A. Haemophilus influenzae
B. Streptococcus pneumoniae
C. Parainfluenza virus
D. Staphylococcus aureus
E. Group A Streptococcus
F. Adenovirus
G. Mycoplasma pneumoniae
H. Epstein-Barr virus
I. Corynebacterium diphtheriae
J. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)

Interpretation of findings:

Supraglottitis/epiglottitis and pharyngeal abscess pose a threat to the airway

and must be differentiated from simple tonsillopharyngitis, which is uncomfortable but not acutely

dangerous. Clinical findings help make this distinction.

With supraglottitis/epiglottitis, there is abrupt onset of severe throat pain and dysphagia, usually with no

preceding URI symptoms. Children often have drooling and signs of toxicity. Sometimes (more often in

children), there are respiratory manifestations, with tachypnea, dyspnea, stridor, and sitting in the tripod

position. If examined, the pharynx almost always appears unremarkable.

Pharyngeal abscess and tonsillopharyngitis both may cause pharyngeal erythema, exudate, or both.

However, some findings are more likely in one condition or another:

visible focal swelling in the posterior pharyngeal area (often with deviation of the uvula)

Although tonsillopharyngitis is easily recognized clinically, its cause is not. Manifestations of viral and

GABHS infection overlap significantly, although URI symptoms are more common with a viral cause. In

adults, clinical criteria that increase suspicion of GABHS as a cause include

Those with ≤ 1 criterion reasonably may be presumed to have viral illness. If ≥ 2 criteria are present, the

likelihood of GABHS is high enough to warrant testing but probably not high enough to warrant

antibiotics, but this decision needs to be patient-specific (ie, threshold for testing and treatment may be

lower in those at risk because of diabetes or immunocompromise). In children,

Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) may also present as ARDS. Hemorrhage can be bland (ie, not associated with vascular inflammation) or owing to capillaritis. In bland DAH, hemorrhage can result when elevated cardiac filling pressures (as in cardiogenic pulmonary edema) occur in the setting of coagulopathy or when contusion follows trauma. Alveolar hemorrhage owing to contusion should be considered when alveolar bleeding is coincident with pneumothorax, pneumatoceles, bony fractures, and cutaneous bruising. In contrast, capillaritis can be provoked by a wide range of insults including anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody–associated or other small vessel vasculitides, connective tissue diseases, anti–glomerular basement membrane disease, certain drugs, and infections.   Hemoptysis is a classic presenting symptom of DAH, although it is absent in at least one-third of patients, and a decrease in hemoglobin may also be observed. DAH is classically diagnosed by BAL showing an increase in red blood cells in serial lavage. Although DAD and DAH may have nearly identical radiologic appearances on the chest radiograph, highly experienced radiologists can sometimes make the diagnosis of DAH based on the differential radiodensity using a CT scan. The identification of DAH does not distinguish between bland hemorrhage and capillaritis, and should be followed by an investigation into the specific cause.

Interpretation of findings:

The distinction between acute and chronic stridor is important. Other clinical

findings are also often helpful (see

).

Acute manifestations are more likely to reflect an immediately life-threatening disorder. With these

disorders, fever indicates infection. Fever plus barking cough suggests croup or, very rarely, tracheitis.

Patients with croup typically have more prominent URI symptoms and less of a toxic appearance. Fever

without cough, particularly if accompanied by toxic appearance, sore throat, difficulty swallowing, or

respiratory distress, suggests epiglottitis and, in young children, the less common retropharyngeal

abscess. Drooling and the tripod position are suggestive of epiglottitis, whereas retropharyngeal abscess

may manifest with neck stiffness and inability to extend the neck.

Patients without fever or URI symptoms may have an acute allergic reaction or aspirated foreign body.

Acute allergic reaction severe enough to cause stridor usually has other manifestations of airway edema

(eg, oral or facial edema, wheezing) or anaphylaxis (itching, urticaria). Foreign body obstruction of the

upper airway that causes stridor is always acute but may be occult in toddlers (older children and adults

can communicate the event unless there is near-complete airway obstruction, which will manifest as such,

not as stridor). Cough is often present with foreign body but rare with allergic reaction.

Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH) may also present as ARDS. Hemorrhage can be bland (ie, not associated with vascular inflammation) or owing to capillaritis. In bland DAH, hemorrhage can result when elevated cardiac filling pressures (as in cardiogenic pulmonary edema) occur in the setting of coagulopathy or when contusion follows trauma. Alveolar hemorrhage owing to contusion should be considered when alveolar bleeding is coincident with pneumothorax, pneumatoceles, bony fractures, and cutaneous bruising. In contrast, capillaritis can be provoked by a wide range of insults including anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody–associated or other small vessel vasculitides, connective tissue diseases, anti–glomerular basement membrane disease, certain drugs, and infections.   Hemoptysis is a classic presenting symptom of DAH, although it is absent in at least one-third of patients, and a decrease in hemoglobin may also be observed. DAH is classically diagnosed by BAL showing an increase in red blood cells in serial lavage. Although DAD and DAH may have nearly identical radiologic appearances on the chest radiograph, highly experienced radiologists can sometimes make the diagnosis of DAH based on the differential radiodensity using a CT scan. The identification of DAH does not distinguish between bland hemorrhage and capillaritis, and should be followed by an investigation into the specific cause.

The distinction between acute and chronic stridor is important. Other clinical

Acute manifestations are more likely to reflect an immediately life-threatening disorder. With these

Both techniques are currently applied in the diagnostic workup of IE and CIED with two main indications: Confirming the presence of infection and identification of septic emboli. By this approach, a substantial reduction in the rate of misdiagnosed IE has been demonstrated. In general, (18F)FDG PET/CT is characterized by higher spatial resolution and sensitivity, better image quality, and shorted acquisition times compared to WBC scan. In contrast, WBC scintigraphy is more specific than (18F)FDG PET/CT, being able to achieve a differential diagnosis between a sterile inflammation, as observed early after surgery. Therefore, WBC imaging should be preferred in all the situations that require higher specificity or in case of inconclusive (18F)FDG PET/CT. Major drawbacks of WBC include the relatively complex and time-consuming labeling procedure that requires a particular equipment, the handling of potentially infected blood, and longer acquisition times. Routine chemistry panel and haemogram were within normal limits. C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 28 g/dl (normal <5) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 30 mm/hour. Empirical treatment with ampicillin-sulbactam and gentamicin was initiated.. Confirmed diagnosis: Staphylococcus warnerii prosthetic valve endocarditis. She had undergone an aortic valve replacement 7 months earlier without postsurgical complications, and cefazolin was administered for 3 days during the perioperative period. Her body temperature was 36.9°C, with blood pressure readings of 114/74 mm Hg on the right arm and 114/81 mm Hg on the left arm. Physical examination showed no conjunctival hemorrhage or cardiac murmur. Laboratory tests indicated an elevated white blood cell count of 8,830/µL and a C-reactive protein level of 10.12 mg/dL. Enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen revealed no abnormalities. Blood cultures were performed due to her medical history and physical examination findings. Four days prior to admission, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis (MRSE) was detected in two sets of blood cultures. Despite recommendations for hospitalization, she chose to go home. Repeated blood cultures again showed MRSE in two sets, leading to her admis. Confirmed diagnosis: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis.

Presentation: A 53-year-old male patient had a mitral valve replacement using a Starr Edwards metal valve. Post-surgery, he experienced acute renal failure and required temporary hemodialysis via a vascular catheter for 36 days. The longest duration a single catheter was used was 13 days. Cultures from four removed vascular catheter tips showed the presence of diphtheroids and coagulase-negative staphylococci, typically considered normal skin flora. During this period, the patient developed a low-grade fever, which subsided after changing the catheters. Blood cultures did not show any growth.. Confirmed diagnosis: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis caused by Corynebacterium jeikeium. Differential diagnosis includes: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis caused by Corynebacterium jeikeium.

Presentation: An 80-year-old female was admitted in March 2012 presenting with fever, low blood pressure, and confusion. Her medical history includes aortic valve replacement with a biological prosthesis and double coronary artery bypass performed in April 2011. Upon admission, blood cultures identified the presence of Staphylococcus lugdunensis. The patient was treated with oxacillin, which led to the resolution of her fever. CT/FDG-PET revealed a diffuse uptake on prosthetic valve (SUVmax 4.2). Two weeks after hospital admission a new TEE showed a peri-valve tissue abscess with aortic vegetation.. Confirmed diagnosis: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis.

The most common indication for TKR is osteoarthritis (OA). In 2018, 96.2% of primary knee replacements were conducted solely due to osteoarthritis. TKR helps to improve quality of life and function in end-stage, symptomatic osteoarthritis patients. However, 10–34% of TKR patients receive adverse pain outcomes between three months and five years following surgery and around 20% of TKR patients experience more knee pain and swelling than before surgery. Despite advancements in surgical techniques, prostheses, pain control, and medical care, there is evidence to suggest worsening pain and functional scores of some patients over time following TKR surgery.

Red Flags 
 Hot, swollen, single joint = septic until proven otherwise → arthrocentesis
 Fever with joint complaints (septic arthritis, endocarditis)
 Prosthetic joint with new pain/swelling (prosthetic joint infection)
 IV drug use + joint pain (hematogenous seeding)
 Polyarthritis + new murmur (endocarditis)
 Pediatric arthritis + fever + rash (consider Kawasaki disease , rheumatic fever , JIA)

Presentation: A 43-year-old woman with a history of aortic valve replacement three years ago presented with a 20-day history of fever and night sweats. Physical examination revealed an axillary temperature of 38.5°C, heart rate of 90/min, blood pressure of 90/70 mmHg, and a diastolic murmur (2/4) at the aortic area. Routine chemistry panel and haemogram were within normal limits. C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 28 g/dl (normal <5) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 30 mm/hour. She had undergone silicon mammoplasty nine months ago and dental extraction four months ago. Three months ago, she was treated with ceftriaxone and gentamicin for four weeks. After one month of discharge, she experienced fever and night sweats again. On the second day of the current hospitalization, painful nodules were observed on the pad of the right index finger. Empirical treatment with ampicillin-sulbactam and gentamicin was initiated.. Confirmed diagnosis: Staphylococcus warnerii prosthetic valve endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Staphylococcus warnerii prosthetic valve endocarditis.

Clinical presentation is typically characterized by the signs and symptoms incorporated in Duke criteria (fever, vascular and immunological phenomena). Nevertheless, elderly patients can have atypical presentations characterized by the absence of fever, pre-existing heart murmurs, or blunted rise of inflammatory markers, resulting in more difficult diagnostic work-up.

Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?

B. *Bartonella henselae*
C. HACEK group organisms
D. *Candida albicans*
E. Beta-hemolytic streptococci
F. *Staphylococcus aureus*
G. Coagulase-negative *Staphylococcus spp.*
H. *Pseudomonas* aeruginosa
I. *Streptococcus bovis*
J. *Enterococcus*

Ventricular arrhythmias following Venus P-Valve implantation have been reported predominantly as transient, early events. In a recent multicenter comparative study by Haddad et al. (2025; n = 145), directly comparing self-expanding Venus P-Valve (n = 52) with balloon-expandable SAPIEN-3 (n = 93) in native or patched RVOTs, procedural success was 100% in both groups and major complication rates were comparable (9.6%, 5/52, in the Venus-P cohort). Transient ventricular arrhythmias occurred more frequently after Venus P-Valve implantation (21.1%, 11/52) compared with SAPIEN-3 (3.2%, 3/93), but all events resolved without catheter ablation or long-term antiarrhythmic therapy, and no sustained ventricular tachycardia or arrhythmic death was reported. Across additional multicenter and registry experiences, sustained ventricular arrhythmias have been uncommon. In the Italian SICPED Registry, transient ventricular ectopy – occasionally short non-sustained ventricular tachycardia – was observed in 19% (12/65) of patients, typically resolving within one month on β-blocker therapy, with no cases of high-grade atrioventricular block, pacemaker implantation, or sudden arrhythmic death at a median 13-month follow-up. In the CE-mark study by Qureshi et al., one patient developed sustained ventricular tachycardia requiring implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation and catheter ablation, without a broader signal of malignant ventricular arrhythmia across the 81-patient cohort. Presentation: A 53-year-old male patient had a mitral valve replacement using a Starr Edwards metal valve. Post-surgery, he experienced acute renal failure and required temporary hemodialysis via a vascular catheter for 36 days. The longest duration a single catheter was used was 13 days. Cultures from four removed vascular catheter tips showed the presence of diphtheroids and coagulase-negative staphylococci, typically considered normal skin flora. During this period, the patient developed a low-grade fever, which subsided after changing the catheters. Blood cultures did not show any growth.. Confirmed diagnosis: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis caused by Corynebacterium jeikeium. Differential diagnosis includes: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis caused by Corynebacterium jeikeium.

Presentation: An 80-year-old female was admitted in March 2012 presenting with fever, low blood pressure, and confusion. Her medical history includes aortic valve replacement with a biological prosthesis and double coronary artery bypass performed in April 2011. Upon admission, blood cultures identified the presence of Staphylococcus lugdunensis. The patient was treated with oxacillin, which led to the resolution of her fever. CT/FDG-PET revealed a diffuse uptake on prosthetic valve (SUVmax 4.2). Two weeks after hospital admission a new TEE showed a peri-valve tissue abscess with aortic vegetation.. Confirmed diagnosis: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis. Differential diagnosis includes: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis.

The most common indication for TKR is osteoarthritis (OA). In 2018, 96.2% of primary knee replacements were conducted solely due to osteoarthritis. TKR helps to improve quality of life and function in end-stage, symptomatic osteoarthritis patients. However, 10–34% of TKR patients receive adverse pain outcomes between three months and five years following surgery and around 20% of TKR patients experience more knee pain and swelling than before surgery. Despite advancements in surgical techniques, prostheses, pain control, and medical care, there is evidence to suggest worsening pain and functional scores of some patients over time following TKR surgery.

Red Flags 
 Hot, swollen, single joint = septic until proven otherwise → arthrocentesis
 Fever with joint complaints (septic arthritis, endocarditis)
 Prosthetic joint with new pain/swelling (prosthetic joint infection)
 IV drug use + joint pain (hematogenous seeding)
 Polyarthritis + new murmur (endocarditis)
 Pediatric arthritis + fever + rash (consider Kawasaki disease , rheumatic fever , JIA)

Although type 1 diabetes also exhibits increased hepatic gluconeogenesis, hyperglucagonemia and hyperglycemia, it is not a risk factor for NAFLD. This can be attributed to the absence of glucagon resistance in type 1 diabetes, as manifested by increased hepatic urea synthesis efficiency. In type 1 diabetes, hyperglucagonemia and associated hyperglycemia occur because of reduced insulin secretion. Notably, hyperinsulinemia, a characteristic of type 2 but not type 1 diabetes, causes reduced plasma adiponectin. On the other hand, patients with type 1 diabetes have increased plasma adiponectin. Adiponectin signaling in hepatocytes activates AMPK and improves insulin sensitivity. AMPK activation should inhibit all the components of glucagon resistance including lipogenesis (Figure 4). AMPK activates endothelial nitric oxide synthase, which produces nitric oxide, which inhibits xanthine oxidase. Hence, type 1 diabetes is also associated with reduced uric acid synthesis.

US is the most validated modality for assessing splenomegaly. The splenic volume is calculated using the formula for a prolate ellipse (0.52 × length × anteroposterior dimension × width). However, given the strong correlation between the splenic length and volume, a simple measurement of the longest dimension along the oblique craniocaudal axis is preferred. In contrast, CT and MRI, which provide images on predefined planes, may underestimate splenic size because of challenges in accurately measuring the longest craniocaudal dimension. Chow et al. conducted a study aimed at defining individualized normal values for splenic length and volume. They found that splenic size correlates with height, weight, and sex: it tends to be larger in taller, heavier individuals and in males. Notably, the frequently cited upper limit of normal for splenic length (12 cm) was exceeded by 26% of males and 6% of females. This finding highlights the need for corrected upper limits to prevent unnecessary workups in otherwise healthy individuals whose splenic length surpasses the published normal values. They also proposed validated algorithms to determine the percentiles of individual splenic sizes and introduced an application to facilitate clinical use (for iOS [https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/splenocalc/id1005559584?mt=8] and Android [https://play.google.com/store/search?q=splenocalc]).

Hyperinsulinism is a medical condition characterized by inappropriately high insulin secretion compared to plasma glucose concentration, leading to a continuous stimulation of hepatic glycogen synthesis and glucose uptake by skeletal muscles and adipose tissue. Hyperinsulinism can be transient, congenital or syndromic. Transient hyperinsulinism is a common cause of severe hypoglycemia in newborns and it can be found in children of diabetic mothers, IUGR, SGA or it can be secondary to perinatal stress. The disease course is usually self-limiting and it is defined by resolution prior to 6 months of age. Hyperinsulinism in infants of diabetic mothers, when diabetes in poorly controlled, is caused by prolonged intrauterine exposure to high blood glucose levels resulting in increased fetal growth and LGA. Immediately after birth, these infants are at high risk for hypoglycemia but, usually, this condition resolves spontaneously in a few days until the beta-pancreatic cells adapt to the normoglycemic state. In addition, gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is associated with long-term complications for offspring including childhood obesity and glucose intolerance. The molecular basis of offspring adiposity and glucose intolerance is expected to be correlated to genetic and epigenetic modifications owing to intrauterine hyperglycemia. In some cases, newborns experience a prolonged state of transient hyperinsulinism. Counter-regulatory hormone deficiencies may be isolated or part of panhypopituitarism. Hypopituitarism should be suspected in children with midline defects (such as cleft lip or cleft palatal), optic nerve hypoplasia and, in males, micropenis. Isolated GH deficiency (GHD) is caused by mutations in the GHRH, GH or their respective receptors. GHD associated with hypopituitarism can be due to central nervous system abnormalities (such as empty sella syndrome, septo-optic dysplasia, pituitary hypoplasia/aplasia) or to acquired causes (such as meningitis, hydrocephalus, radiotherapy, head injury, cerebral infarction, cancer, and surgery). GHD leads to decreased lipolysis and glycogenolysis. Metabolic effects of GHD are represented by ketotic hypoglycemia associated with fasting metabolic acidosis. However, in infants, it presents with a clinical picture identical to that of hyperinsulinism (hypoglycemia associated with low/normal levels of ketone bodies and fatty acids, absence of metabolic acidosis and positive response to glucagon administration). Other clinical features are prolonged and recurrent jaundice in infants, early and progressive growth deceleration during the first years of life, and dysmorphic features with midline defects (in hypopituitarism) occur. The treatment is hormone-replacement therapy; in cases of persistent hypoglycemia, GH treatment can be initiated during the neonatal period with daily subcutaneous injections of recombinant human GH in the evening to mimic the physiological release of GH. Familial chylomicronemia syndrome, characterized by the accumulation of extremely high levels of chylomicrons and in many cases VLDL is the result of inherited deficiencies in key factors in the pathways of TRL assembly and clearance. One of the best characterized of these disorders is absence of functional lipoprotein lipase (LpL) activity in which VLDL catabolism is severely impaired, in particular the lipolysis of VLDL1 (Figure 3). In experiments using tracers of radio-iodinated VLDL1 and VLDL2 in subjects with the condition, it was observed that the FCR of VLDL1 was decreased 10-fold but apoB production into this lipoprotein fraction was similar to normal. VLDL2 clearance, on the other hand, was not significantly impaired by lack of LpL. Deficiency of the other key lipase in lipoprotein metabolism—hepatic lipase (HL)—is associated with hypertriglyceridemia but not to the same extent as seen in LpL deficiency. Investigations reveal that this enzyme is more active at hydrolyzing lipid in smaller particles in the VLDL2, IDL, and LDL density intervals. HL deficient subjects exhibit reduced clearance rates for VLDL and IDL, and slowed conversion of VLDL2 to IDL and IDL to LDL (Figure 3). In the subject we studied there was an almost complete inability to convert IDL to LDL.

Presentation: A 1-year-old Sri Lankan boy was brought to the pediatric service for evaluation and treatment of an upper respiratory tract infection. He was the second child, born at 38 weeks of gestation via normal vaginal delivery after an uneventful pregnancy to healthy, nonconsanguineous parents. His birth and neonatal period were unremarkable, and he was exclusively breastfed. On physical examination, the infant exhibited mild hepatomegaly with a liver palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin. Blood samples taken during the assessment were noted to be grossly lipemic. There were no signs of eruptive xanthomas or epigastric abdominal pain; however, fundoscopy showed lipemia retinalis. His elder sister was in good health. The mother had a history of dyslipidemia diagnosed at 30 years of age and was on lipid-lowering therapy. Liver and renal function tests were normal, as was serum uric acid, but plasma lactate was elevated at 27.3 mg/dL (reference range: 4.5-19.8). A complete blood count revealed mild microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed mild hepatomegaly and moderate splenomegaly.. Confirmed diagnosis: Lipoprotein Lipase Deficiency. Differential diagnosis includes: Lipoprotein Lipase Deficiency.

Vertical SGP (especially downward) is a key feature of Niemann–Pick type C (NPC), present in 65%. NPC is an autosomal-recessive illness caused by mutations in the NPC1 or NPC2 gene, in which cholesterol and lipids accumulate due to a defect in intracellular lipid trafficking. Additional features include gelastic cataplexy and hepatosplenomegaly, although in adult-onset cases, visceromegaly may be absent.

Physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests, including blood work, renal function, electrolyte levels, and routine urine analysis, all returned normal results.. Confirmed diagnosis: Congenital absence of the sacrum. Differential diagnosis includes: Congenital absence of the sacrum.

Presentation: A 16-day-old female infant presented with bilious vomiting and absence of meconium passage. No antenatal ultrasonography was conducted, and there was no reported maternal drug intake during pregnancy. The baby was delivered at home via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 1.3 kg, and was in a sick and dehydrated state upon admission. Vital signs included a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per minute, a pulse rate of 150 beats per minute, and a blood pressure reading of 80/60 mmHg. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal distention with a soft abdomen and no rigidity. The anal opening was normally positioned. Laboratory results showed a normal haemogram, but serum urea and creatinine levels were moderately elevated.. Confirmed diagnosis: Congenital Absence of Jejunum and Ileum. Differential diagnosis includes: Congenital Absence of Jejunum and Ileum.

payload.vignette:
A 4-month-old male infant is evaluated during a routine well-child check. The parents report difficulty weaning him from nighttime feedings, noting that he becomes extremely distressed after 3-4 hours without feeding and is only consoled by being fed.

Growth assessment reveals a decline from the 25th to the 5th percentile in length, while weight remains at the 25th percentile. Physical examination reveals distinctive facial fullness, significantly distended abdomen, and thin limbs. The liver edge extends to the iliac crest, but the spleen is not enlarged.

A blood sample demonstrates a characteristic milky white layer on its surface.

Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?

Options:
A. Prader-Willi syndrome
B. Congenital hyperinsulinism
C. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency
D. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency
E. Gaucher disease
F. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency
G. Glycogen storage disease type 1
H. Tay-Sachs disease
I. Familial hypercholesterolemia
J. Niemann-Pick disease type A

expected to extend about 2 cm beneath the costal margin for each 1-g decrease in Hb. Other clinical

findings usually result from the underlying disorder.

Although type 1 diabetes also exhibits increased hepatic gluconeogenesis, hyperglucagonemia and hyperglycemia, it is not a risk factor for NAFLD. This can be attributed to the absence of glucagon resistance in type 1 diabetes, as manifested by increased hepatic urea synthesis efficiency. In type 1 diabetes, hyperglucagonemia and associated hyperglycemia occur because of reduced insulin secretion. Notably, hyperinsulinemia, a characteristic of type 2 but not type 1 diabetes, causes reduced plasma adiponectin. On the other hand, patients with type 1 diabetes have increased plasma adiponectin. Adiponectin signaling in hepatocytes activates AMPK and improves insulin sensitivity. AMPK activation should inhibit all the components of glucagon resistance including lipogenesis (Figure 4). AMPK activates endothelial nitric oxide synthase, which produces nitric oxide, which inhibits xanthine oxidase. Hence, type 1 diabetes is also associated with reduced uric acid synthesis.

US is the most validated modality for assessing splenomegaly. The splenic volume is calculated using the formula for a prolate ellipse (0.52 × length × anteroposterior dimension × width). However, given the strong correlation between the splenic length and volume, a simple measurement of the longest dimension along the oblique craniocaudal axis is preferred. In contrast, CT and MRI, which provide images on predefined planes, may underestimate splenic size because of challenges in accurately measuring the longest craniocaudal dimension. Chow et al. conducted a study aimed at defining individualized normal values for splenic length and volume. They found that splenic size correlates with height, weight, and sex: it tends to be larger in taller, heavier individuals and in males. Notably, the frequently cited upper limit of normal for splenic length (12 cm) was exceeded by 26% of males and 6% of females. This finding highlights the need for corrected upper limits to prevent unnecessary workups in otherwise healthy individuals whose splenic length surpasses the published normal values. They also proposed validated algorithms to determine the percentiles of individual splenic sizes and introduced an application to facilitate clinical use (for iOS [https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/splenocalc/id1005559584?mt=8] and Android [https://play.google.com/store/search?q=splenocalc]).

Presentation: A 16-day-old female infant presented with bilious vomiting and absence of meconium passage. No antenatal ultrasonography was conducted, and there was no reported maternal drug intake during pregnancy. The baby was delivered at home via normal vaginal delivery, weighing 1.3 kg, and was in a sick and dehydrated state upon admission. Vital signs included a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per minute, a pulse rate of 150 beats per minute, and a blood pressure reading of 80/60 mmHg. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal distention with a soft abdomen and no rigidity. The anal opening was normally positioned. Laboratory results showed a normal haemogram, but serum urea and creatinine levels were moderately elevated.. Confirmed diagnosis: Congenital Absence of Jejunum and Ileum. Differential diagnosis includes: Congenital Absence of Jejunum and Ileum.

The surgery was completed under spinal anesthesia, and a male neonate was delivered with a birthweight of 3.47 kg and a length of 51 cm. There were no complications during pregnancy, and all prenatal sonographic exams were normal. The newborn examination showed no dysmorphism. Entamoeba hiatolytica, which causes amoebic colitis, is another IBD mimicker that can cause bloody diarrhea. Endoscopic findings include skip lesions and multifocal ulceration, which is more common on the right side of the colon and can mimic CD. Microbiologically, the diagnosis of amoebiasis can be made by stool microscopy and periodic‐acid Schiff (PAS) positive trophozoites on biopsy. Histologically, there are flask‐shaped ulcers with florid necroinflammatory exudate, erythrophagocytosis, cryptitis, lamina propria‐containing chronic inflammatory infiltrates, surface epithelial damage, and PAS stains highlight the organisms. In contrast to IBD, the mucosa adjacent to the amoebic ulcers is normal, with an absence of granuloma. Of note, chronic amoebic infection can lead to crypt distortion and fibrosis, which could mimic IBD.

Presentation: Patient A, a 31-year-old woman, visited the hospital on 1 June 2017 due to 'fatigue and dizziness for 1 month and worsening for 1 week.' The patient experienced dizziness and fatigue without any clear cause 1 month prior, with symptoms intensifying over the past week. She sought care at the emergency department. Blood tests revealed a hemoglobin (HGB) level of 38 g/L, and esophagogastroduodenoscopy indicated chronic superficial gastritis. Despite blood replenishment treatment, severe anemia persisted, and symptoms of dizziness and fatigue showed minimal improvement. Consequently, the patient was admitted for 'anemia of unknown origin.' During her hospital stay, she did not report nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, abdominal distension, black stool, or bloody stool. Physical examination noted an anemic appearance, a soft abdomen without tenderness or rebound pain, no palpable masses, and bowel sounds occurring six times per minute. Admission findings included anemia of unknown origin. Blood tests showed HGB at 45 g/L; urine analysis revealed 94 RBC/μl; stool occult blood test was positive; and tumor marker tests indicated erythropoietin levels >762.00 mIU/ml. Contrast-enhanced CT sca. Confirmed diagnosis: Small Intestinal Lymphangioma. Differential diagnosis includes: Small Intestinal Lymphangioma.

Presentation: A 38-year-old male with a history of type III intestinal failure due to chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction related to gastrointestinal dysmotility, cardiac and intestinal arrhythmia syndrome, dependence on parenteral nutrition, sinus dysfunction, and a pacemaker. The patient has chronic intestinal insufficiency due to a motor disorder of the intestines and has been part of an intestinal rehabilitation program requiring regular monitoring of nutritional, biometric, and electrolytic parameters. The patient was admitted to a high-complexity hospital presenting with diffuse, mild-intensity abdominal pain for six days and multiple vomiting episodes. There was no fever, diarrhea, jaundice, or other associated symptoms. Vital signs upon admission were: blood pressure 98/54 mmHg, heart rate 67 per minute, respiratory rate 16 per minute, and oxygen saturation 95%. Physical examination showed an alert and oriented patient with mild dehydration, minimal tenderness upon abdominal palpation, and no clear signs of peritoneal irritation. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed intestinal obstruction with a transition zone in the jejunum, without signs of complications or intestinal loop. Confirmed diagnosis: Wernicke's Encephalopathy. Differential diagnosis includes: Wernicke's Encephalopathy.

Presentation: Patient A, a 31-year-old woman, visited the hospital on 1 June 2017 due to 'fatigue and dizziness for 1 month and worsening for 1 week.' The patient experienced dizziness and fatigue without any clear cause 1 month prior, with symptoms intensifying over the past week. She sought care at the emergency department. Blood tests revealed a hemoglobin (HGB) level of 38 g/L, and esophagogastroduodenoscopy indicated chronic superficial gastritis. Despite blood replenishment treatment, severe anemia persisted, and symptoms of dizziness and fatigue showed minimal improvement. Consequently, the patient was admitted for 'anemia of unknown origin.' During her hospital stay, she did not report nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, abdominal distension, black stool, or bloody stool. Physical examination noted an anemic appearance, a soft abdomen without tenderness or rebound pain, no palpable masses, and bowel sounds occurring six times per minute. Admission findings included anemia of unknown origin. Blood tests showed HGB at 45 g/L; urine analysis revealed 94 RBC/μl; stool occult blood test was positive; and tumor marker tests indicated erythropoietin levels >762.00 mIU/ml. Contrast-enhanced CT sca. Confirmed diagnosis: Small Intestinal Lymphangioma. Differential diagnosis includes: Small Intestinal Lymphangioma.

Presentation: A 38-year-old male with a history of type III intestinal failure due to chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction related to gastrointestinal dysmotility, cardiac and intestinal arrhythmia syndrome, dependence on parenteral nutrition, sinus dysfunction, and a pacemaker. The patient has chronic intestinal insufficiency due to a motor disorder of the intestines and has been part of an intestinal rehabilitation program requiring regular monitoring of nutritional, biometric, and electrolytic parameters. The patient was admitted to a high-complexity hospital presenting with diffuse, mild-intensity abdominal pain for six days and multiple vomiting episodes. There was no fever, diarrhea, jaundice, or other associated symptoms. Vital signs upon admission were: blood pressure 98/54 mmHg, heart rate 67 per minute, respiratory rate 16 per minute, and oxygen saturation 95%. Physical examination showed an alert and oriented patient with mild dehydration, minimal tenderness upon abdominal palpation, and no clear signs of peritoneal irritation. A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan revealed intestinal obstruction with a transition zone in the jejunum, without signs of complications or intestinal loop. Confirmed diagnosis: Wernicke's Encephalopathy. Differential diagnosis includes: Wernicke's Encephalopathy.

A 5-year-old female child is brought to a medical office with complaints of progressive abdominal pain that has intensified in the last 24 hours. The father reports a history of constipation, with no bowel movement for the past 72 hours and no bloody stools. She has experienced three episodes of vomiting since the previous night and is refusing food. Her medical and surgical history is unremarkable. Physical examination reveals upper abdominal distention with tympany, but no abdominal mass, involuntary guarding, or rebound tenderness is detected. What is the most probable underlying etiology of her clinical presentation?

A. Hirschsprung disease
B. Intestinal lymphoma
C. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome
D. Chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction
E. Volvulus
F. Malrotation of the gut

H. Intussusception

knowledge_chunks.text: Presentation: A 26-year-old female (primigravida) underwent an emergency cesarean section at 40 weeks after failed induction. The surgery was completed under spinal anesthesia, and a male neonate was delivered with a birthweight of 3.47 kg and a length of 51 cm. There were no complications during pregnancy, and all prenatal sonographic exams were normal. The newborn examination showed no dysmorphism. Post-C-section, the baby was transferred to the nursery for routine care and feeding. However, 24 hours post-delivery, the baby was moved to the neonatal intensive care unit due to poor feeding, bilious vomiting, and abdominal distension. Physical examination revealed normal vitals, persistent abdominal distension upon palpation, sluggish movements, and bloody mucoid stools. The baby was put under nil by mouth, and a nasogastric tube was inserted, revealing a light greenish aspirate. An x-ray showed multiple loops of dilated small bowel indicating obstruction. Intravenous fluids were started, and antibiotics (amoxicillin 50 mg every 12 hours and gentamicin 5 mg every 48 hours) were administered due to the possibility of bowel necrosis and perforation. The case was referred to pediatric surgery, and . Confirmed diagnosis: Hirschsprung’s disease. Differential diagnosis includes: Hirschsprung’s disease.

Entamoeba hiatolytica, which causes amoebic colitis, is another IBD mimicker that can cause bloody diarrhea. Endoscopic findings include skip lesions and multifocal ulceration, which is more common on the right side of the colon and can mimic CD. Microbiologically, the diagnosis of amoebiasis can be made by stool microscopy and periodic‐acid Schiff (PAS) positive trophozoites on biopsy. Histologically, there are flask‐shaped ulcers with florid necroinflammatory exudate, erythrophagocytosis, cryptitis, lamina propria‐containing chronic inflammatory infiltrates, surface epithelial damage, and PAS stains highlight the organisms. In contrast to IBD, the mucosa adjacent to the amoebic ulcers is normal, with an absence of granuloma. Of note, chronic amoebic infection can lead to crypt distortion and fibrosis, which could mimic IBD.

The diagnostic criteria for CdLS were published by the Medical Director of the CdLS Foundation (Kline et al. ), categorizing the CdLS phenotype into cardinal and suggestive features. Cardinal features, each assigned a score of 2 if present, include synophrys/thick eyebrows, short nose/concave nasal ridge/upturned nasal tip, long/smooth philtrum, thin upper lip vermilion/downturned corners of mouth, hand oligodactyly/adactyly, and ongenital diaphragmatic hernia. Suggestive features are assigned a score of 1 each if present and include global developmental delay/intellectual disability, prenatal growth retardation < 2SD, postnatal growth retardation < 2SD, prenatally/postnatally microcephaly, small hands/ft, short fifth finger, and hirsutism. Individuals with a score of ≥ 11 and at least 3 cardinal features are classified as having classic CdLS. Those with a score of 9–10 and at least 2 cardinal features are classified as having non‐classic CdLS. A score of 4–8 with at least 1 cardinal feature warrants molecular testing for CdLS, whereas a score of < 4 is insufficient to indicate the need for such testing.

Presentation: A 13-year-old male was referred to our department with chest pain, chest deformity, and myopia. The chest pain had been occurring for 5 years, lasting approximately 5 minutes each time. There were no associated palpitations, autonomic symptoms, presyncope or syncope, and the pain was not related to respiration or food intake. Family history revealed that the patient's maternal great-uncles were tall and thin. On physical examination, the patient appeared comfortable at rest, was tall (1.75 m, 97th percentile), and thin with features including long fingers and toes (arachnodactyly), sunken chest (pectus excavatum), long limbs (dolichostenomelia), positive wrist and thumb signs, increased arm span relative to height, elongated head (dolichocephaly), spinal curvature (scoliosis), downward-slanting eye openings (downslanting palpebral fissures), underdeveloped cheekbones (malar hypoplasia), and keloid formation. His total systemic score was 8 based on specific criteria. Laboratory tests, including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, calcium, magnesium and phosphate, and liver function tests, were within normal limits.. Confirmed diagnosis: Marfan syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Marfan syndrome.

Case 2 A third pregnancy was spontaneously conceived some years later. The first trimester scan was normal, with a nuchal translucency of 1.2 mm and a low risk for major aneuploidies at combined test. At 16 weeks, fetal biometry and anatomy were normal. The couple was referred to our hospital at 21 weeks because of the recurrence of FGR. At ultrasound examination FGR was confirmed and multiple morphological abnormalities, similar to those of the first deceased baby, were reported: the hands were clenched during the whole time of the examination with abducted fingers (Fig. 1a); there was a right rocker-bottom foot with plantar edema (Fig. 1b); both superior and inferior limbs were constantly extended with no evidence of flexion-extension at joints; the lenses were bilaterally hyperechoic, suggestive for cataract, and the orbital diameter was bilaterally below the 5th centile (Fig. 1c); slight retrognathia and low implantation of the ears were also reported (Fig. 1d). A multidisciplinary counselling was performed during which the parents were informed regarding the poor prognosis; the likelihood of a hereditary condition and the possibility of a COFS syndrome were hypothesized. The amniocentesis was performed. As first-tier genetic test, we performed a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP’s) array analysis (ILLUMINA Express Exome arrays) and metabolic investigations, including the measurement of 7-dehydrocholesterol, in order to detect any chromosomal molecular abnormality and to exclude the Smith–Lemli–Opitz Syndrome (SLOS).
